lessons.plain: Target sizing means working out how much computing power, memory and disk a business application such as SAP will need once it runs in the cloud, before you reserve anything. It is like planning how big a kitchen must be before opening a restaurant: too small and service slows down, too large and you pay for empty space. For SAP, you start from the measured load of the current system, such as how many users work in it and how much data it holds, then convert that load into the size of virtual machines and disks that can carry it, with room for growth. The estimate is a starting point that you check with testing, not a final answer.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your SAP system runs on an old physical server with 64 CPU cores and 1 TB of memory, and it feels busy at month end. Is copying those exact numbers to a cloud virtual machine a safe sizing decision? Explain your reasoning in a few sentences.
lessons.teach:
A vCPU is one virtual processor core that a cloud virtual machine (VM) is given. A core count alone does not tell you how much SAP work a machine can do, so SAP sizing uses SAPS, the SAP Application Performance Standard, a unit SAP uses to rate how much dialog and batch work a set of application servers can process. SAP HANA is an in-memory database that keeps its working data in RAM, so for HANA the memory size is usually the deciding factor, and the memory must hold the data plus working space. A certified VM is a VM size that SAP has approved for a given workload type and that has a known SAPS rating or memory capacity. Why this works: you convert a measured or forecast load into the capacity units the cloud sells, then pick the smallest certified size that covers it with headroom.

Worked example. Suppose the sizing input says the application servers need 9,000 SAPS and the HANA database holds 400 GB of data. Step 1: the application tier needs 9,000 SAPS. Step 2: add 30 percent growth, giving 11,700 SAPS. Step 3: a candidate VM is rated 4,000 SAPS, and 11,700 divided by 4,000 is 2.9, so you round up to 3 VMs. Step 4: for HANA, choose a memory-rich certified VM whose memory is well above 400 GB, leaving room for working space and growth, and check the exact figures against the current certified list.

Common mistake: copying the old server's core count and memory, which ignores that the old box may be idle most of the year and that month-end peaks set the real demand. Consequence in a running system: an undersized HANA VM runs out of memory under peak load, and users see slow dialog responses or failed batch jobs during closing.

Good sizing starts from measured peak load, converts it into SAPS and memory, and adds headroom before choosing a certified VM.

questions.prompt: A retail company is sizing its SAP application tier. Its measured peak load is 6,500 SAPS, the SAP Application Performance Standard unit that rates dialog and batch work. Step 1: the application tier needs 6,500 SAPS at peak. Step 2: add 20 percent growth, giving 7,800 SAPS. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: the candidate certified VM is rated 2,500 SAPS, so the team has 4 VMs in the design. Which completes the missing step 3?
choices: Divide 7,800 SAPS by 2,500 SAPS to get 3.12, then round up to 4 VMs
Multiply 7,800 SAPS by 2,500 SAPS to get the total VM capacity needed
Round 3.12 down to 3 VMs because a fraction of a machine is not needed
Divide the original 6,500 SAPS by 2,500 to get 2.6 and round down to 2 VMs
questions.why: Dividing the grown load by one VM's rating gives the number of machines needed, and any fraction is rounded up so the capacity still covers the load.

questions.prompt: In SAP sizing, what does the SAPS unit measure?
choices: The amount of RAM a database keeps in memory
The disk input and output speed of the storage volume
The number of physical CPU sockets installed in a server
The rate of dialog and batch work that application servers can process
questions.why: SAPS is the SAP Application Performance Standard, a unit that rates how much dialog and batch work a set of application servers can process.

questions.prompt: A team has an SAP HANA database holding 300 GB of data. They choose a certified VM with 320 GB of memory because it just fits the data. What is the main problem with this choice?
choices: HANA cannot run on any VM with more than 256 GB of memory
A VM with memory just above the data size is fine because HANA stores only the data
The VM will have too many vCPUs for the database to use efficiently
Memory must hold the data plus working space and growth, so 320 GB leaves too little room and risks running out under peak load
questions.why: HANA keeps its working data in RAM, so memory must cover the data, working space and growth, and a size that only just fits can run out of memory at peak.

questions.prompt: A team measures its SAP application servers at an average of 1,200 SAPS across the month but a month-end peak of 5,000 SAPS. Which figure should drive the target sizing?
choices: The 5,000 SAPS peak plus headroom, since month-end peaks set the real demand
The lowest daily reading, so the design does not pay for idle capacity
The sum of the two figures divided by two, to balance the average and peak
The 1,200 SAPS average, since it reflects normal daily use
questions.why: Good sizing starts from measured peak load and adds headroom, because peaks such as month-end closing determine whether the system stays responsive.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate proposes sizing the new SAP HANA virtual machine by copying the CPU and memory of the current on-premises server. In your own words, explain how you would estimate the target size instead, and name one limit or tradeoff of your estimate.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would not copy the old server, because its CPU and memory numbers describe what it was built for, not what the workload needs. I would start from measured peak load, such as month-end activity, and from the database size, then convert the application load into SAPS and size the HANA database by its memory need, which must hold the data plus working space. I would add headroom for growth and pick the smallest certified VM that covers both figures. The main limit is that this is still a forecast. Peak behaviour can differ after migration, and a new version or more users can change the load, so I would check the estimate with a performance test before committing to a reservation.
rubricPoints: Sizes from measured or forecast peak load, not the old server's hardware
Converts application load into SAPS and sizes HANA mainly by memory
Adds headroom for growth and selects a certified VM size
Names a real limit, such as forecast error, and recommends testing to validate

suggested.rationale: Choosing a target size means reasoning through a scenario with competing figures, which an exam-style situation practises better than a read-only summary, though no listed mission covers this yet.

lessons.plain: When a company moves its SAP business software into the cloud, not every combination of software and hosting is a supported one. A supported scenario is a specific arrangement that the software vendor and the cloud provider both agree will run properly and that they will help with if something breaks. Think of a car warranty: the manufacturer only covers the engine if it was built with approved parts and fuel. This objective is about recognising which arrangements are on the approved list, such as SAP applications running on virtual machines in Azure, or a fully managed SAP setup called RISE. Checking support first saves you from building something nobody will help you fix later.
lessons.guessPrompt: If your company runs an SAP system on a server in the cloud, what would you check before you trust that the vendor will help you if it breaks?
lessons.teach:
A supported scenario is a deployment combination that the software vendor (SAP) and the platform provider (Microsoft Azure) both document as allowed for production use. The combination has several parts: the SAP product and release (for example S/4HANA or an older NetWeaver-based ERP), the database underneath it (often SAP HANA), the operating system, the virtual machine size, and the hosting model. Each part has its own approved list, and a deployment is supported only when every part sits on its list together.

Two hosting models matter most here. In the first, you run SAP yourself on Azure virtual machines, which are rented servers you configure and control, so your team owns the operating system, the database and the SAP patching. In the second, SAP RISE is a managed offering in which SAP runs the landscape for you on Azure and you consume it as a service. Which model fits is decided by the vendor support matrix and the cloud provider's SAP documentation, not by what seems technically possible.

Worked example: a team wants to run S/4HANA with a HANA database on Azure. Step one: confirm the SAP release is on the vendor's supported list. Step two: confirm that the HANA version and the operating system version appear together in the vendor's compatibility listing. Step three: pick a virtual machine size that is certified for the memory the HANA database needs. Step four: confirm the hosting model is a standard virtual machine deployment or a managed RISE offering, not an unlisted custom setup. If any step fails, the scenario is unsupported, even if the software installs and starts.

Common mistake: assuming that a deployment which boots and passes a quick test is supported. Support is an agreement between vendors, and an unlisted combination can leave you without help during an outage.

Consequence: when a production incident happens on an unsupported combination, the vendor may refuse to investigate until the landscape is moved onto a listed configuration, which can extend downtime for the business. Confirming support before design work begins is therefore a planning step, not paperwork.

questions.prompt: A regional bakery chain plans to run an older NetWeaver-based ERP with a HANA database on standard Azure virtual machines that its own team will patch. The architect has already confirmed two things: the NetWeaver release appears on the vendor's supported list, and the HANA version and the Linux version appear together in the vendor's compatibility listing. The architect has not yet checked the planned virtual machine size against the vendor's certified sizes for the database memory the bakery needs, which is estimated at 1.5 TB. Which remaining check decides whether this scenario is supported?
choices: Confirm that the planned virtual machine size is certified for the memory the HANA database needs
Confirm that the bakery's peak order volume stays within the virtual machine's CPU count
Ask the vendor to pre-approve the custom monitoring agent the team wants to install
Check that the bakery's ERP has a nightly backup window long enough for its sales data
questions.why: Support requires every part of the combination, including the virtual machine size, to sit on its approved list, and that size check is the step still outstanding.

questions.prompt: In the managed hosting model described for SAP on Azure, who runs the SAP landscape day to day?
choices: The customer's own team, which owns the operating system, the database and the SAP patching
SAP, which runs the landscape for the customer on Azure and the customer consumes it as a service
The Azure platform team alone, with SAP providing only licence keys
A third-party contractor chosen by the customer, with no role for SAP
questions.why: In the SAP RISE managed model, SAP runs the landscape on Azure and the customer consumes it as a service, while self-run virtual machine deployments put operating system, database and patching ownership on the customer's team.

questions.prompt: A team builds an S/4HANA system on a combination the vendor has not listed. It installs, starts, and passes a quick functional test. What is the correct conclusion?
choices: The deployment is supported once the team documents the test results for the vendor
The deployment is supported only if the virtual machine is larger than the minimum size
The deployment is supported because it passed a functional test
The deployment is unsupported, because a working test does not establish that the vendor and Azure both allow the combination for production
questions.why: Support is an agreement between vendors covering the whole combination, so a deployment that merely boots and passes a test can still be unsupported for production.

questions.prompt: A company runs a HANA database on a certified virtual machine size, with a Linux version that is on the operating system list, but the HANA version and that Linux version do not appear together in the vendor's compatibility listing. Is the scenario supported?
choices: Yes, because each part is individually on an approved list
No, because every part must sit on its list together, and this pairing is not listed
No, but only if the company is running S/4HANA rather than another SAP product
Yes, because the virtual machine size compensates for the missing pairing
questions.why: A deployment is supported only when every part, including the specific database and operating system pairing, is on the approved listing together, so an unlisted pairing makes the whole scenario unsupported.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide whether a proposed SAP deployment on Azure is a supported scenario, and name one limit of that check.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would check each part of the proposed stack against the current vendor and cloud provider listings: the SAP product release, the database and its version, the operating system, and the virtual machine size. All of them must appear together as a supported combination, and the hosting model must be one the provider documents for SAP, such as standard virtual machines or a managed RISE offering. The limit is that these listings change over time, so I would confirm against the current versions on the day of the decision rather than relying on memory. A listed scenario is also only necessary, not sufficient: sizing, licensing and cost still have to be worked out separately before the design is approved.
rubricPoints: Support depends on the whole combination: product, database, operating system, VM size and hosting model.
Vendor and cloud provider documentation is the source of truth, checked against current versions.
Two common hosting models are self-run SAP on Azure virtual machines and managed SAP RISE.
A deployment that merely runs is not thereby supported.
Support status is necessary but not sufficient for a design decision.

suggested.rationale: Supported-scenario checks are a catalogue and support-matrix fact that no listed mission or planned engine currently exercises, so reading the teaching text is the best fit.

lessons.plain: Before you can run an SAP system in the cloud, you have to write down what it needs: how much processing power and memory each server needs, how fast its disks must read and write, and how the servers must talk to each other and to users. These needs are called requirements. An SAP system is usually several servers working together, such as application servers that run the business logic and a database server that holds the data, so each part has its own needs. Good requirements let you choose a server size, disk type and network layout that fit the job, instead of guessing and paying for the wrong thing.
lessons.guessPrompt: An SAP system has one database server and two application servers that users connect to. Users report that screens are slow to save, but the application servers' CPU is low. Which requirement would you check first on the database server, and why might a bigger CPU not fix it?
lessons.teach:
Start with the definitions. A requirement is a measurable need that a workload places on infrastructure. For SAP, the requirements fall into three groups. Compute means CPU cores and memory. Storage means disks, measured in input and output operations per second (IOPS), throughput in megabytes per second, and latency, which is how long a single request takes to finish. Network means bandwidth, the delay between components, and which ports and paths must be open. SAPS is SAP's own benchmark-based figure for application-server processing power, used to size the application tier. An in-memory database such as SAP HANA is sized mainly from the volume of data it must hold in memory, not from CPU count.

Why this works: each SAP tier has a different profile. Application servers can be added in number and need moderate CPU and memory. The database tier depends on memory size and on low disk latency for its log, because each committed change must be written to the log before the work is confirmed. Central services hold locks and messages. They are small but a failure there stops everything.

Worked example: a 2 TB HANA database. Step 1: take the memory requirement from the data volume and add headroom, so the server offers clearly more RAM than the data needs. Step 2: pick a server family that appears on the SAP-supported list for HANA. Step 3: put the log on its own low-latency disk, separate from the data files. Step 4: size the application servers from SAPS estimated for the user count, and place them in the same region and network segment as the database so round trips stay short.

Common mistake: sizing from CPU count alone, or placing data, log and shared files on one generic disk. Consequence in a running system: a database short on memory slows down or fails to load, and commits slow because log writes queue behind other disk traffic. Users feel this as slow saves, even when the application servers look idle.

questions.prompt: A regional food distributor is moving its SAP ERP system to Azure. Its SAP HANA database holds 1.2 TB of data, and the team has chosen a server with clearly more memory than that. The team estimates 18,000 SAPS for peak load, and the chosen application-server VM is rated at 4,500 SAPS on the sizing list. The plan for sizing the application tier is: Step 1, take the 18,000 SAPS need. Step 2, [missing]. Step 3, place the application servers in the same region and network segment as the database. Which choice correctly fills Step 2?
choices: Multiply 18,000 by 4,500 to get the number of servers needed
Divide 18,000 by 4,500 to get 4 application servers
Use the database memory size of 1.2 TB as the server count
Count the named users and assign one server per 100 users, ignoring SAPS
questions.why: Dividing the required SAPS by the SAPS rating of one VM gives the number of application servers, which is the sizing method the teaching text describes.

questions.prompt: In SAP infrastructure planning, what does the latency of a storage requirement measure?
choices: The megabytes per second a disk can move
The number of network ports that must be open between tiers
How long a single request takes to finish
The number of operations a disk completes each second
questions.why: The teaching text defines latency as how long a single request takes to finish, distinct from IOPS and throughput.

questions.prompt: A team needs to host a new HANA database that holds 3 TB of data. Which sizing approach fits the teaching text?
choices: Pick a VM by CPU count, since CPU drives HANA sizing
Store data, log and shared files together on one premium disk for simplicity
Choose a server with clearly more memory than 3 TB and confirm it appears on the SAP-supported HANA list
Use the application tier's SAPS rating to set the database memory
questions.why: An in-memory database is sized mainly from the data volume it must hold, with headroom, and the server should be on the SAP-supported list for HANA.

questions.prompt: After the database log was moved onto a shared disk that also serves other workloads, users report slow saves while the application servers look idle. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The application servers have too few CPU cores to process the save requests
The central services lock table is too small for the number of users
Each committed change must wait for its log write, which queues behind other disk traffic and raises commit latency
The application servers were placed in a different region from the users
questions.why: Commits wait on log writes, so contention on a shared disk raises latency for every save, which matches the consequence the teaching text describes.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate which requirements you would gather for an SAP database server and for its application servers before choosing Azure virtual machine sizes and disks. Name one limit or tradeoff in how far you can trust those numbers before a load test.
lessons.modelAnswer: For the database server I would gather the data volume, because an in-memory database needs enough RAM to hold it with headroom, and I would check that the server family is on SAP's supported list. I would also gather the log write latency target, so the log gets its own low-latency disk. For the application servers I would estimate SAPS from the number of users and their typical transactions, and I would keep them in the same region and network segment as the database. The limit is that these numbers are estimates built from user counts and growth assumptions. Real behaviour, such as month-end batch peaks or custom code, can differ a lot, so I would treat the sizing as a starting point and confirm it with a load test before go-live.
rubricPoints: Names compute, storage and network as the three requirement groups
Explains that the database tier depends on memory sized from data volume and on low log latency
Explains that application servers are sized from SAPS and can scale out
States that estimates need validation with testing because real load can differ

suggested.rationale: Explaining which requirements each SAP tier needs is the core skill here, and no listed mission covers SAP sizing.

lessons.plain: When you move a large SAP system into the cloud, you cannot simply ask for as many servers as you like. Your cloud account is split into subscriptions, which are containers that hold resources, carry a bill, and define who can change things. Each subscription also has quotas, which are caps on how much of each kind of resource you may use in each region. Before you plan an SAP landscape, you check whether the subscription you will use can actually get the machines the design needs, in the place you want them, and how long getting more capacity would take. Finding a limit late can delay a go-live by weeks.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a company has a big budget and wants twelve large database servers next month, what might stop them from getting all twelve straight away, even with money available?
lessons.teach:
A subscription is the unit Azure uses for billing, access control and resource limits. The resources an SAP landscape needs, such as virtual machines, disks and network addresses, are created inside one subscription in one region. A quota is the cap the platform sets on how much of a resource type a subscription may hold in a region. For virtual machines, the most important quota is the number of vCPUs, the processor cores a machine uses. Quotas are counted separately for each VM family, which is a group of machine sizes with the same hardware profile. SAP databases such as SAP HANA usually need large memory-optimised sizes from a few families, so the quota for those families can block a deployment even when the overall regional total looks fine. Quotas can often be raised by a request, but approval takes time and is not guaranteed for every size.

Worked example. A design needs four database VMs of 128 vCPUs each from one family, so 512 cores in that family. The subscription's quota for that family in the chosen region is 256. Step one: the planner sees that 512 is more than 256, a gap of 256 cores. Step two: they either request a quota increase of at least 256 cores, choose a region with capacity, or check whether a smaller size still meets the sizing. Step three: they record the request, its expected lead time and a fallback in the migration plan before any cutover date is set.

Common mistake: checking only total regional vCPUs, or assuming production and test share one pool. Each subscription has its own limits, so one heavy test environment can use up the cores production needs.

Consequence: a deployment that fails partway through leaves a half-built landscape, and a blocked quota pushes the cutover date back for every team waiting on it. The subscription boundary also decides who may change the limits, so the request must go to whoever owns the account, which under a managed model such as SAP RISE may be SAP or its managed-service partner rather than the customer.

questions.prompt: Northwind Foods plans six database VMs of 96 vCPUs each, all from one VM family in one region, so the family needs 576 cores. The subscription's quota for that family in that region is 400 cores. Step one: the team confirms the requirement is 576 cores. Step two: they compare it with the 400-core quota and find a gap of 176 cores. Step three is missing. Which action completes the planning step correctly?
choices: Record the quota increase request, its expected lead time and a fallback option in the migration plan before the cutover date is fixed.
Halve the vCPUs on each VM and skip recording anything, since a smaller size always avoids the quota problem.
Assume the account's overall regional total covers the 176-core gap, because that total is larger than 576.
Move cores from the company's test subscription into production so the gap closes without any approval.
questions.why: The planning step is to write down the request, its lead time and a fallback before setting any cutover date, because quotas are per subscription and per family and cannot be assumed to be covered by other totals.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes a quota in this context?
choices: The cap the platform sets on how much of a resource type a subscription may hold in one region.
The list of named people allowed to change the subscription's settings.
The total amount billed to a subscription in one month.
The number of resources an operator is allowed to delete in a day.
questions.why: A quota is the platform-set limit on how much of one resource type a subscription can hold in a given region, which is the definition given in the teaching text, restated in plain words.

questions.prompt: Lumen Retail needs eight VMs of 64 vCPUs each from one VM family in one region for its production SAP database. Its separate test subscription in that same region already holds most of that family's quota. Production's deployment fails, although the region's overall vCPU total looks sufficient. What best explains this?
choices: Quotas only apply to storage and network addresses, so the vCPU count cannot block a deployment.
Azure automatically blocks any deployment that would take more than half of a region's capacity, whatever the subscription.
Production and test draw from one shared pool of cores in the region, so the failure must come from a disk limit instead.
Quota is counted per subscription and per VM family, so the test subscription's use of that family can leave production without enough cores.
questions.why: Each subscription has its own limits counted per VM family, so heavy test use can exhaust the family quota that production needs even when the regional total looks fine.

questions.prompt: A customer engineer under a managed model such as SAP RISE finds that a cutover is blocked by a vCPU quota and wants to raise it. Which is the right first move?
choices: Open a quota request in the customer's own subscription without checking who owns it, because quota is always the customer's to change.
Delete the test VMs to free cores in the subscription, then tell the owner afterwards.
Switch the SAP sizing to a smaller VM family and reschedule the cutover without telling the owner.
Confirm who owns the subscription under the managed model, then send the quota request to that party with the lead time and fallback recorded.
questions.why: The subscription boundary decides who may change limits, and under a managed model the owner may be SAP or its managed-service partner, so the request must go to that party.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says we can deploy the SAP production VMs now and sort out capacity later. Explain to them why subscription and quota limits must be assessed during planning, naming one limit or tradeoff that makes raising a quota less than a free fix.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would tell them that quotas are checked before deployment because a failed or partial deployment leaves the landscape broken and the cutover date slips. We need to count the vCPUs per VM family in the target subscription and region, not just the overall regional total, because SAP database sizes often come from a few families with small quotas. If we are short, a quota increase is a request that needs approval and has a lead time we do not control, and the approved region may not have the family we need. So the tradeoff is that asking for more capacity can be slow, and moving to another region can add latency between SAP application and database servers. We should raise the request in planning and record a fallback.
rubricPoints: Quotas are per subscription, per region, and per VM family, so totals alone are misleading
Quota increases need approval and lead time that the team does not control
Checking limits during planning avoids partial deployments and cutover delays
A tradeoff exists: a different region may lack capacity or add latency between SAP tiers

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine covers subscription quotas, and the core skill here is explaining the constraint and its tradeoff to a teammate.

lessons.plain: When you run software, someone has to give you the right to use it, and that right is called a license. An SAP system on a cloud virtual machine usually needs several licenses at once: one for the SAP application, one for the operating system, and one for the database underneath. Some come from SAP itself, some from the operating system vendor, and some can be covered by licenses your company already owns. Before you build or price a server, list each product on it and find out who grants the right to run it, because moving to the cloud does not remove those obligations. Getting this wrong can mean unexpected bills or a failed license audit.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team copies an SAP server into the cloud and finds the monthly bill includes Windows and SQL Server charges they previously paid under a separate agreement for their own hardware. Why might that happen, and what should they have checked before moving?
lessons.teach: Software licensing is the set of rights that let you run a piece of software, and for SAP workloads on Azure it has several separate layers that must each be identified before you size or price anything. The first layer is the SAP license itself: a contract with SAP that defines how many users or how much database capacity your SAP system may use. It is agreed with SAP, not with the cloud provider, and moving to Azure does not remove it. The second layer is the operating system, such as Windows Server or a Linux distribution like Red Hat or SUSE. You can pay for it per hour inside the cloud image price, or bring a subscription you already own. The third layer is the database, such as SQL Server on Windows or SAP HANA, each with its own counting rules. A useful test is to list every product on the virtual machine stack and ask who grants the right to run it and how that right is counted. Worked example. A team plans a Windows virtual machine running SQL Server for an SAP database. Step 1: list the products, which are Windows Server, SQL Server and the SAP application. Step 2: check whether the company already holds Software Assurance, which is an add-on maintenance right, on its Windows Server and SQL Server licenses. Step 3: if it does, apply Azure Hybrid Benefit to those virtual machines so the existing rights cover the Windows and SQL charges instead of paying the cloud image rate again. Step 4: keep the SAP license as a separate item, because the hybrid benefit does not cover it. Common mistake: assuming that because the cloud bill includes the operating system, the SAP and database rights are also covered. They are not. Consequence: in a running landscape, a virtual machine on a paid image without a matching license risks audit findings and surprise cost, and a system built with the wrong rights may need rebuilding.

questions.prompt: A retailer runs an SAP ERP application on SUSE Linux virtual machines, with an SAP HANA database on the same stack. Step 1: list the products on the stack: SUSE Linux, SAP HANA, and the SAP ERP application. Step 2: the retailer already owns SUSE subscriptions and wants to avoid paying the cloud image rate for Linux. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: the SAP ERP contract with SAP stays on the list as its own item, because it is agreed with SAP and not with the cloud provider. What completes Step 3?
choices: Ask the cloud provider to confirm in writing that the SAP ERP contract is covered by the Linux image price.
Treat the SAP HANA database as covered, since SUSE is part of the stack and its rights extend to the database.
Remove the SAP ERP item from the list, since the cloud bill already includes the operating system.
Apply the existing SUSE subscriptions to those virtual machines so the rights the retailer already owns cover the Linux charge instead of the image rate.
questions.why: Step 3 is where the retailer decides how the operating system right is supplied, and bringing an owned subscription to the virtual machines is the option the teaching text describes for the operating system layer.

questions.prompt: A company moves its SAP system from its own data centre to Azure. Which statement about the SAP license is correct?
choices: The SAP license is agreed with the cloud provider, which takes over the SAP contract during migration.
The SAP license only matters for the operating system, so it can be dropped once the database is moved.
The SAP license is replaced by the cloud provider's pay-as-you-go rate, so no separate SAP contract is needed.
The SAP license is still a contract with SAP that sets user or database capacity, and moving to Azure does not remove it.
questions.why: The teaching text says the SAP license is agreed with SAP, defines user or database capacity, and is not removed by moving to Azure.

questions.prompt: A team builds a Linux virtual machine on a paid image to run an SAP HANA database. They reason that because the image price includes Linux, the HANA database rights are also covered. What is the correct response?
choices: The reasoning is correct, because the database is installed on the same virtual machine as the operating system.
The reasoning is wrong: the image price covers only the operating system, and the database has its own rights and counting rules that must be checked separately.
The reasoning is correct only if the team uses the hybrid benefit on the virtual machine.
The reasoning is wrong only if the virtual machine runs in a region outside the team's home country.
questions.why: Each product on the stack has its own licensing layer, so a cloud image price for the operating system does not automatically cover the database, and the team must identify the database rights separately.

questions.prompt: A company holds Software Assurance on its Windows Server licenses but no Software Assurance on its SQL Server licenses. It plans Windows virtual machines running SQL Server for an SAP database. Which plan fits the licensing layers in the teaching text?
choices: Skip the SQL Server licensing step, since SQL is part of the SAP database and is covered by the SAP license.
Apply the hybrid benefit to cover the Windows Server charge, and keep the SQL Server charge as a separate licensing item that still needs its own rights.
Pay the cloud image rate for SQL Server through the virtual machine, since the hybrid benefit is only for Windows.
Apply the hybrid benefit to all the virtual machines, which covers both the Windows and SQL charges because the company already has Software Assurance.
questions.why: The hybrid benefit uses existing rights, and the teaching text ties it to Software Assurance on both Windows and SQL, so the Windows charge can be covered while the SQL charge still needs a matching right.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would work out which software licenses a new SAP virtual machine on Azure needs, and name one limit or tradeoff of the approach you would take.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by listing every product on the stack: the SAP application, the database, and the operating system. For each one I would ask who grants the right to run it and how it is counted, whether by users, by database capacity, or by virtual cores. Then I would check what the company already owns. If it has Software Assurance on Windows Server or SQL Server, I can apply Azure Hybrid Benefit so those existing rights cover the cloud charges. The tradeoff is that this only works for products the company already licenses; the SAP contract is separate and still needs to be confirmed with SAP. Also, the hybrid benefit depends on the counting method, so a sizing change later can change the license need. I would record the decisions with the sizing so the team can audit them later.
rubricPoints: Lists each product on the stack and who grants its license
Explains that the SAP license is separate from the operating system and database rights
Describes Azure Hybrid Benefit as applying existing Windows or SQL rights with Software Assurance
Names a limit, such as the SAP contract not being covered or licenses changing with resizing

suggested.rationale: Licensing rules are contract and catalogue facts that are best learned by reading the layered explanation rather than by a listed mission.

lessons.plain: Moving a business system to the cloud changes what you pay, and not always in the way people expect. Some costs follow how many machines run and how big they are. Others follow the storage you keep, the data that leaves the cloud network, and the copies kept for recovery. Identifying cost implications means listing every part of the target setup, deciding which parts you pay for by the hour, which you pay for by the month, and which grow quietly over time. A good estimate catches the costs that are easy to forget before the bill arrives.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose you move a database server from your own data centre to a cloud virtual machine that runs all day, every day. Name two costs you would pay for beyond the machine itself, and say which one would surprise you most.
lessons.teach:
A cost implication is the effect a design choice has on what you pay over time. Start with the main terms. A virtual machine is a rented server, billed while it runs at a rate set by its size and region. Pay-as-you-go means you pay the list rate with no commitment. A reservation is a commitment to a fixed amount of capacity for one or three years in exchange for a lower rate. Managed disks are storage volumes attached to a machine, billed by size and performance tier. Egress is data leaving a region or network, often charged per gigabyte. A snapshot is a point-in-time copy of a disk, billed for the space it holds.

Why it works: a total cost is the sum of compute hours, storage held, data moved, and services kept running. Each has its own driver, so you estimate them separately and then add them up.

Worked example: a sizing decision needs a machine with a fixed memory footprint. Step 1: the machine runs 730 hours a month at a list rate, giving the compute line. Step 2: the data disks hold 2 TB on a premium tier, billed per month, giving the storage line. Step 3: a standby copy in a second region runs continuously, so it adds a second compute line for that role. Step 4: nightly backups create snapshots that accumulate for thirty days, giving the backup line. Step 5: the total is compute plus disks plus replica plus backup, with replication traffic leaving the region added as egress on top.

Common mistake: estimating only the machine's hourly rate and forgetting the disks, replicas, backups and data transfer, which together can make up a large share of the total.

Consequence: if a disaster-recovery replica is priced as though it were idle when it actually runs continuously, the monthly bill is understated, and the team meets the real figure at the first invoice rather than during planning.

questions.prompt: A retail company is pricing a new SAP quality system. Step 1: the two application servers run 730 hours a month at the list rate, which gives the compute line. Step 2: 3 TB of data disks on a premium tier, billed monthly, gives the storage line. Step 3: the database replica in a second region is shut down on weekends, so it runs 480 hours a month and is billed only for those hours, giving a second compute line. Step 4 is missing. Step 5: the total is the sum of all the lines, with any data leaving the region added on top. Which choice correctly fills Step 4?
choices: Count the nightly snapshots as a backup line, billed for the space they hold over fourteen days.
Drop the replica line because it is shut down on weekends, so it adds nothing to the total.
Divide the storage line by the number of servers to get a per-machine rate.
Multiply the compute line by 0.6 to apply a reservation discount to the whole total.
questions.why: Snapshots are a separate billed item, priced by the space they hold while they accumulate, so Step 4 must add that backup line to the total.

questions.prompt: In cost terms, what does a reservation require from the buyer?
choices: Renting disks by the hour so that their size can be changed freely during the year.
A commitment to a fixed amount of capacity for one or three years, in exchange for a lower rate.
Paying the list rate with no end date and cancelling at any time without penalty.
Paying only for the space that snapshots hold, billed per gigabyte per month.
questions.why: A reservation is a fixed-term commitment to a set amount of capacity that buys a lower rate, which is what the second choice describes.

questions.prompt: A steady production database server will run 24 hours a day for the next three years with no planned shutdowns. Which billing choice is most likely to lower its compute cost?
choices: Moving the server's disks to a cheaper region with no change to how the server is billed.
Pay-as-you-go, because having no commitment is always the cheapest option.
Pay-as-you-go combined with a scheduled daily stop for the server.
A three-year reservation covering that capacity, which lowers the rate for the committed hours.
questions.why: Because the server runs continuously for the full term, a reservation for that capacity lowers the rate, whereas pay-as-you-go keeps the higher list rate.

questions.prompt: A team estimates a migration's monthly cost using only the hourly rate of two virtual machines. Which items are most likely missing from that estimate?
choices: Only the operating system licence, since that is the sole cost not covered by the hourly rate.
Managed disks, snapshots kept for backup, and data leaving the region, each billed separately.
The reservation discount, which must be subtracted from the total as a fixed amount.
Nothing, because the hourly rate already includes the disks, backups and data transfer.
questions.why: Disks, snapshots and egress each have their own billing driver and are not included in a machine's hourly rate, so the estimate understates the total.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would estimate the monthly cost of a new SAP database landscape on Azure, and name one limit or tradeoff of your estimate.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would split the landscape into the things that bill differently. First, compute: each virtual machine's size and region at the list rate for the hours it runs, with the production and standby machines both counted if the standby runs continuously. Second, storage: the size and performance tier of each managed disk, plus snapshot or backup retention over the period. Third, data transfer, especially replication traffic that leaves a region. Then I would add these together and compare against any reservation that would lower the compute line. The main limit is that the estimate is only as good as the sizing assumptions behind it. If the real workload needs a larger machine or more storage than planned, or if traffic patterns differ from what I assumed, the actual bill will move. I would state those assumptions next to the number so the team can revisit them.
rubricPoints: Separates compute, storage, backup or snapshot, and data transfer costs
Counts always-on standby or disaster-recovery resources at their running cost
Notes that commitments such as reservations change the compute rate
Names a limit: the estimate depends on sizing and usage assumptions that may change

suggested.rationale: A planned cost model engine would let the learner build and vary a multi-part estimate, which is the core skill this objective tests.

lessons.plain: A support plan is the paid agreement that decides how help reaches you when something breaks in your cloud account. Think of it like choosing between basic roadside cover and premium cover: both exist, but they differ in how quickly someone answers, how urgent a problem must be before it gets fast attention, and whether a skilled technical engineer works the problem with you instead of only answering billing questions. For a business system that other teams depend on, choosing the tier is a planning decision made alongside sizing and cost, not something to add after go-live.
lessons.guessPrompt: A production SAP system stops working at 2 a.m., and you suspect the cloud platform rather than SAP itself. What would you need from your support arrangement that a free or basic tier might not give you, and why?
lessons.teach:
A support plan is a paid service agreement with the cloud provider. It is bought for an Azure subscription or billing account, and it sets three things: how quickly the provider first responds to a case, how cases are ranked by severity, and who on your side can open cases and reach technical engineers. Severity means how urgent a problem is for the business, usually running from critical (a production system is down) down to low (a general question). Response time is the target for the first reply, and it differs by plan and severity. Production means the live system people depend on; non-production means test and development systems. A basic tier mainly covers billing and quota questions, not technical troubleshooting.

Why it matters: the plan does not repair anything or change your systems. It sets how fast a skilled person starts working on your problem. The tier you choose should therefore match how critical the landscape is, just as you size compute to the workload.

Worked example. A team runs a production SAP database on Azure. At 02:00 the database virtual machine becomes unreachable. Step 1: the on-call engineer classifies the case as critical, because order processing has stopped. Step 2: they open the case through the portal under the subscription that hosts production. Step 3: the plan's critical-severity route brings in a technical engineer within the plan's response target. Step 4: the cloud engineer and the team work the infrastructure side while SAP Basis staff handle the application side.

Common mistake: assuming the cloud support plan covers everything in the SAP landscape. Azure support covers Azure resources; SAP software issues remain under the SAP support agreement, so the two must be planned together.

Consequence: if production runs on a basic tier, the first reply to a critical outage may wait far longer, and the recovery time promised to the business is at risk before anyone has touched the system. A support plan is part of the availability design.

questions.prompt: Lumen Logistics runs a production SAP BW reporting server on Azure. On Monday at 07:00 the server becomes unreachable, and month-end reports cannot be produced. Step 1: the on-call lead classifies the case as critical, because the business cannot produce reports. Step 2: the lead opens the case through the portal under the subscription that hosts the production BW server. Step 3: [missing step]. Step 4: the cloud engineer works the virtual machine while the SAP Basis team checks the BW application layer.
choices: The team waits for the SAP software vendor to confirm the severity before the Azure case is ranked, so both cases stay linked.
The critical-severity route brings a technical engineer in within the plan's response target for that severity.
The team reopens the case under the non-production subscription so it joins the standard queue used for test systems.
The team restarts the server themselves first and only logs the case if the restart fails, so the response clock does not start.
questions.why: The plan's critical-severity route is what brings a technical engineer in within the response target, which is the step the scenario is missing.

questions.prompt: A startup believes its paid support plan will automatically patch and repair its Azure virtual machines whenever they fail. Which statement corrects this belief?
choices: A support plan repairs failed virtual machines automatically, but only during business hours in the region where they run.
A support plan patches the operating system on every virtual machine, while repairs to application code remain the customer's job.
A support plan replaces failed virtual machines with new ones, and the customer pays only for the replacement compute.
A support plan sets how quickly skilled people begin working on a case; it does not repair or change the systems themselves.
questions.why: The teaching text states that a plan does not repair anything or change systems; it governs how fast a skilled person starts working on the problem.

questions.prompt: A company runs a non-production SAP sandbox and a production SAP order system on Azure, and both are covered by one basic tier plan. The production system is the one the business depends on daily. Which change best fits the plan's purpose?
choices: Remove the plan entirely, because basic tiers already cover technical troubleshooting for every system.
Match the production system's plan tier to how critical the landscape is, because a basic tier mainly covers billing and quota questions and may delay the first reply to an outage.
Keep the single basic tier, because the sandbox and production share one subscription and the cost is lower.
Move the sandbox to a higher tier, since non-production systems are the ones that need the fastest first response.
questions.why: The tier should match how critical the landscape is, and a basic tier mainly covers billing and quota rather than technical troubleshooting, so production needs a tier suited to outages.

questions.prompt: A team's Azure support case is closed because the database virtual machine is confirmed healthy at the infrastructure level. The SAP application still throws errors in order processing. What is the correct next step?
choices: Treat the application errors as an SAP software issue, which sits under the SAP support agreement, and plan the two agreements together.
Ask Azure support to reopen the case and keep working the application errors under it.
Restart the database virtual machine again, since a healthy infrastructure check means the application fault is a hardware fault.
Escalate the application errors to the highest severity under the Azure plan so an engineer reviews the SAP code.
questions.why: Azure support covers Azure resources, while SAP software issues remain under the SAP support agreement, so the two must be handled together rather than through the Azure case alone.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what an Azure support plan is, how you would choose one for a production SAP landscape, and name one limit or tradeoff of your choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: A support plan is a paid agreement with the cloud provider that sets response targets by severity, the channels for opening cases, and whether we get access to technical engineers rather than only billing help. For a production SAP landscape I would not choose a basic tier. I would match the plan to how critical the systems are: production needs a plan with fast response for critical cases and technical engineer access, while development systems can use a lower tier. The main tradeoff is cost, because higher tiers add a recurring charge that must be planned in the budget. Another limit is scope: the cloud plan covers Azure resources, so SAP application defects still go through the SAP support agreement. We should document both routes in the runbook so the on-call team knows where to start.
rubricPoints: Defines a support plan as a paid agreement covering response targets, severity levels and who can open cases
Explains that the tier should match how critical the workload is, with production treated differently from non-production
Names a limit or tradeoff such as recurring cost or the boundary between Azure support and SAP support
States that the plan does not fix the system but speeds access to skilled help during an outage

suggested.rationale: Plan tiers, response targets and prices are current catalogue facts best learned by reading the provider's plan comparison.

lessons.plain: Moving a business system to the cloud is a bit like moving house. One option is to pack everything and unpack it unchanged in the new place. That is quick, but the same old furniture comes along. Another option is to move and also replace something while you are at it. For SAP systems, the choice is between moving the system exactly as it is (lift and shift), moving it while also changing the database underneath it, and moving it while converting the database to SAP HANA, a fast in-memory database. The right choice depends on what you need to change, how much downtime you can accept, and whether the current database is supported on Azure.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company runs an SAP system on its own servers with an older database. It wants the system in Azure quickly, with no change to the SAP software or the database. Which option fits best: a plain lift and shift, or a lift-shift-migrate to HANA? Explain your reasoning in one or two sentences.
lessons.teach:
A lift and shift, also called a rehost, copies the SAP application servers and database server to Azure virtual machines (rented virtual servers) with the same operating system, database engine, and SAP release. Very little changes, so the risk and the project effort are low. A lift-shift-migrate adds a change to the platform during the move, such as a different database engine or operating system. A lift-shift-migrate to HANA converts the database to SAP HANA, an in-memory database that keeps data in RAM for speed. SAP's Database Migration Option (DMO) is a common tool for this, because it can move the system and convert the database in one run, but it needs a planned downtime window and a supported starting release.

Why it works: every change you add to the move adds testing and risk, but may remove work you would otherwise do later. A plain lift and shift defers the database decision.

Worked example: an SAP ERP system runs on an older database on-premises, and the goal is HANA. Step 1: confirm the current release and operating system are supported for HANA on Azure virtual machines. Step 2: if they are not, a plain lift and shift first, then an upgrade later, is the safer sequence. Step 3: if they are, a lift-shift-migrate to HANA using DMO can run in a single planned outage, followed by functional testing.

Common mistake: treating the HANA target as a simple copy. The database conversion is a separate project with its own testing, and the outage can be longer than the file copy suggests.

Consequence: a plain lift and shift leaves the old database in place. If that database is out of support, the risk moves to Azure with the system and stays there until someone migrates it.

The choice is about how much change you accept during the move, and a HANA target always means the database conversion is part of the plan.

questions.prompt: A regional distributor runs an SAP ERP system on Microsoft SQL Server in its own data centre and wants to finish on SAP HANA in Azure. Its ERP release and operating system are on the supported list for HANA on Azure virtual machines, so the team plans a lift-shift-migrate to HANA using SAP's Database Migration Option (DMO), which is a tool that moves the system and converts the database in one run. Step 1: confirm the release and operating system are supported for HANA on Azure. Step 2: choose the single-run DMO path because the release supports it. Step 3: left for you to supply. Step 4: schedule functional testing before go-live and keep the source system intact for rollback until the business signs off.
choices: Move the database to a different operating system first, so that the conversion becomes a simpler job.
Skip functional testing, because DMO has already converted the data and no further checks are needed.
Estimate the outage from the file copy time alone, since the database conversion is usually quick.
Estimate the outage window including the database conversion, and plan testing around that window.
questions.why: The database conversion is a separate piece of work that can make the outage longer than the file copy suggests, so the outage window must include it and the testing must fit around it.

questions.prompt: A company copies its SAP application servers and database server to Azure virtual machines. It keeps the same operating system, the same database engine and the same SAP release, and changes nothing else during the move. Which approach is this?
choices: A lift-shift-migrate to HANA
A database conversion followed by a release upgrade
A lift-shift-migrate that changes the operating system
A lift and shift, also called a rehost
questions.why: A lift and shift, or rehost, moves the servers to Azure virtual machines with no platform change, which is exactly what the scenario describes.

questions.prompt: A firm moves its SAP BW system to Azure and, during the same move, switches the database engine from Oracle to Microsoft SQL Server, keeping the SAP release unchanged. Which category does this fall into?
choices: A lift-shift-migrate to HANA
A lift-shift-migrate that changes the database engine
A plain upgrade with no move involved
A lift and shift with no platform change
questions.why: A lift-shift-migrate adds a platform change, such as a different database engine, during the move, and switching from Oracle to SQL Server is such a change, although the target is not HANA.

questions.prompt: A team plans to convert an SAP system to HANA using DMO in a four-hour planned window. They estimate the outage by timing a 300 GB file copy, which takes about 40 minutes, and conclude the window is safe. What is the main flaw in their reasoning?
choices: A 300 GB copy always finishes in under an hour, so the estimate is correct.
DMO cannot run inside any planned outage window at all.
It ignores the database conversion, which can take far longer than the copy.
They should have chosen a plain lift and shift, which has no outage.
questions.why: A HANA target means the database conversion is part of the plan, and its time must be included in the outage estimate because it can exceed the file copy time.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide between a plain lift and shift and a lift-shift-migrate to HANA for an SAP system. Name one limit or tradeoff of the option you would not choose.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start by checking the current release, operating system, and database against what Azure virtual machines and HANA support. A plain lift and shift copies the system with the same database engine and SAP release, so it is the lowest-risk move and the fastest to finish. Its limit is that the old database stays in place, so if that database is near end of support or the business wants HANA, that work is still ahead. A lift-shift-migrate to HANA, usually with SAP's Database Migration Option, combines the move with the database conversion. The tradeoff is a longer planned outage and a separate round of functional testing, and it only works from a supported starting release. So if the release is too old, I would not choose HANA now; I would lift and shift first and schedule the conversion afterwards.
rubricPoints: A plain lift and shift keeps the current database and SAP release, so it carries the lowest change risk.
A lift-shift-migrate to HANA converts the database during the move and needs a supported starting release.
The HANA option usually means a longer planned downtime and a separate functional test cycle.
Choose based on supported versions, the acceptable outage, and whether the old database is still supported.

suggested.rationale: Choosing between these options is a decision under constraints, so reasoning through an exam-style migration scenario adds the most, and no current OpsForge mission covers SAP migration.

lessons.plain: Moving an SAP system to the cloud is not one job with one method. You can carry the same system over almost unchanged, change the database underneath it, or hand the whole running system to a managed provider. Choosing a migration strategy means deciding how much of the system has to change. Choosing a tool means picking the software that measures or moves it. A tool that finds and measures existing servers helps you plan, while a tool that copies data or disks across does the actual move. The right pair depends on what the business needs to keep, what it can afford to change, and how much downtime it can accept.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company runs an SAP system on its own servers and wants it running in Azure within six months with as little change as possible to how it works. Before any teaching, which would you guess is the safer first step: redesigning the system on new components, or copying the existing servers across as they are? Say why.
lessons.teach:
A migration strategy is the decision about how much of the system changes during the move. A rehost, often called lift and shift, copies the existing servers and their software to new virtual machines (VMs, which are software-defined computers) with little or no change. A replatform changes the underlying platform, for example the database. A managed offering, such as SAP RISE, means a provider runs the system for you under a contract. A migration tool is software that does one job in the process. A discovery and assessment tool inventories the current servers and estimates the size of the target VMs. A replication tool keeps a copy of a disk or VM in sync until you switch over. An SAP-side tool, such as a system copy or database migration tool run through SAP's installer, changes the SAP data itself.

The strategy comes first because it decides which tools are even relevant. If nothing about the database changes, a database conversion tool is unnecessary. Worked example: an SAP ERP system on Oracle must reach Azure in one quarter, and the business forbids changes to the application. Step 1: confirm that the database and SAP version stay the same, so the strategy is a rehost. Step 2: run a discovery tool such as Azure Migrate to inventory servers and size the VMs. Step 3: replicate the disks with a replication tool, test the copy, then switch over in a planned downtime window.

Common mistake: choosing the tool before the strategy, such as running a database conversion because it is familiar. This adds change, risk, and downtime that the business did not ask for. The consequence in a running system is real: if sizing data is wrong, the VMs are undersized and the SAP application slows under load after cutover.

The strategy sets how much change happens, and the tool must match that strategy and the allowed downtime.

questions.prompt: A regional paper manufacturer runs an SAP BW reporting system on SQL Server in its own data centre. It must leave the data centre within six months, and the reporting team has said the database and BW release must not change in this wave. Step 1: confirm that the database engine and SAP release stay the same, so the strategy is a rehost. Step 2: run a discovery and assessment tool to inventory the 6 servers and estimate the size of each target VM. Step 3 is missing. Which step completes the plan?
choices: Replicate the server disks with a replication tool, test the copies, then switch over in a planned downtime window.
Choose each VM size from the on-premises CPU count alone, without checking memory or disk throughput.
Run the SAP database migration tool to convert the SQL Server database to SAP HANA before cutover.
Skip testing and switch users over on the first night, since the strategy is already chosen.
questions.why: A rehost with no database change is completed by replicating the disks, testing the copies, and cutting over in a planned window, while the other options add change or skip checks the strategy does not call for.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm wants its SAP system kept running, patched, and operated by a provider under a contract, and it has no internal staff to run the platform. Which strategy fits this requirement?
choices: A rehost, where the existing servers are copied to VMs with no change
A managed offering, such as SAP RISE, where the provider runs the system under contract
A discovery and assessment run, which inventories servers and estimates VM sizes
A replatform, where the database is changed to a different engine
questions.why: A managed offering is the strategy in which a provider operates the system for you under a contract, which is exactly what the firm asked for.

questions.prompt: A food distributor must move its SAP system to Azure with no change to the application code and no database change, and it can accept about two hours of downtime at cutover. Which kind of tool fits this strategy?
choices: A replication tool that keeps copies of the disks in sync until the switchover
A code refactoring tool that rewrites custom ABAP programs for the cloud
An SAP-side database conversion tool that changes the stored SAP data format
No tool is needed, because a rehost always works without any preparation
questions.why: A rehost with a bounded downtime window fits a replication tool that keeps disks in sync until switchover, while a conversion tool would add the change the business ruled out.

questions.prompt: A discovery report under-counted the peak memory of a three-server SAP landscape, and the target VMs were sized from that report without correction. What is the most likely result after cutover?
choices: The replication tool stops keeping the disks in sync and the copies go stale
The application slows under load because the VMs are undersized for real demand
The managed offering charges fall because fewer resources are provisioned
The SAP database converts itself to a smaller format and the system speeds up
questions.why: Wrong sizing input produces undersized VMs, and the SAP application then slows under load after cutover, which is the consequence the teaching text warns about.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate proposes moving our SAP system to Azure by first moving it to a managed SAP RISE offering because it looks simpler. Explain how you would decide between keeping the system largely as it is and moving to a managed offering, and name one limit or tradeoff of each choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by asking what the business needs to keep and what it can change. If the team needs the same SAP version, custom add-ons, and control over the database and operating system, a rehost is the closer fit. Its limit is that we still run and patch the platform ourselves, and we inherit any current server design problems. A managed RISE offering moves operations to the provider, which reduces our platform work, but we give up some control over configuration and must fit our processes to their service model. Before choosing either, I would run an assessment tool to size the current workload and confirm the downtime window, because those facts often decide which option is realistic.
rubricPoints: Ties the strategy choice to what the business must keep or can change.
Names a discovery or assessment step and says what it measures.
States a tradeoff for the rehost, such as continued platform operations.
States a tradeoff for the managed offering, such as less control over configuration.
Mentions downtime or sizing as a constraint on the choice.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine practises migration strategy or tool selection, so the core material is reading the decision logic and its terms.

lessons.plain: Authorization and access control decide who can do what to which resources. In Azure, you grant people and services a role at a scope, such as one resource group or a whole subscription, and that role lists the actions allowed. For SAP workloads this covers two layers: who may manage the Azure machines, disks and networks that host SAP, and who may use the SAP system itself. Good design gives each person only the access their job needs, granted at the smallest scope that works.
lessons.guessPrompt: A consultant needs to restart SAP application servers in one resource group, but must not be able to change network rules or delete database disks. Would you grant access on the whole subscription, on that resource group, or on each individual disk, and why?
lessons.teach:
A role is a named bundle of allowed actions, such as reading or restarting virtual machines. A role assignment connects a principal to a role at a scope. A principal is whoever receives access: a user, a group, or a managed identity, which is an identity Azure creates for a resource so it can call other services without a stored password. A scope is the level where the grant applies. Azure scopes nest: a management group contains subscriptions, a subscription contains resource groups, and a resource group contains resources. A grant at a higher scope flows down to everything beneath it, and multiple assignments add together. This is Azure role-based access control (RBAC), which governs the Azure resources themselves. Permissions inside the SAP application, such as user roles and authorizations, form a separate layer that you must design too.

Why it works: for each request, Azure asks whether any assignment held by the caller, at the target's scope or above it, includes the needed action. If none does, the request is refused.

Worked example: a group called sap-basis-ops holds a role that allows starting and stopping virtual machines, assigned at the resource group rg-sap-prd. An engineer asks to restart the application server vm-app01, which lives in rg-sap-prd. Step 1: Azure finds the engineer's group membership. Step 2: it finds the assignment at rg-sap-prd, which sits above vm-app01. Step 3: the role includes restart, so the request is allowed. A request to edit a network security rule in the same group is refused, because no assignment includes that action.

Common mistake: granting a broad role such as Owner or Contributor at subscription scope because it is quicker than finding the right scope. Every resource in that subscription, including the production database host and its network, then inherits that power.

Consequence: one careless command or one compromised account can stop production SAP or alter the network paths SAP depends on. Least privilege, meaning the narrowest role at the lowest scope the job requires, keeps that damage small.

questions.prompt: Northwind Health has an automation identity called id-report-sched, a managed identity attached to the VM vm-report03 in resource group rg-claims-test. A role that allows starting virtual machines is assigned to id-report-sched at the subscription sub-claims-test. The identity asks to start vm-report03. Step 1: Azure finds the assignments held by id-report-sched. Step 2: Azure identifies the target's scope and every scope above it, which are rg-claims-test and sub-claims-test. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: Because the role includes the start action, the request is allowed.
choices: It checks only the permissions stored on the VM itself and ignores assignments at higher scopes.
It asks the identity for its stored password before deciding whether the start request is allowed.
It allows the request automatically because the identity is a managed identity, without looking at any role.
It checks whether any assignment at those scopes includes the start action, and the role does include it.
questions.why: Azure checks every assignment at the target's scope or above for the needed action, and the subscription-level assignment includes start, which is what step 3 must state.

questions.prompt: In Azure role-based access control, which of the following is a principal?
choices: A managed identity that Azure creates for a resource to call other services
A scope such as a subscription or management group
A resource group that holds several virtual machines
A role definition that bundles allowed actions such as reading or restarting
questions.why: A principal is whoever receives access, and a managed identity is an identity Azure creates for a resource, while the other options are a container, a bundle of actions, and a level where grants apply.

questions.prompt: A contractor holds the Contributor role only at resource group rg-sap-dev. They ask to change a network security rule on a resource in rg-sap-prd. What happens, and why?
choices: The request is refused, because no assignment at rg-sap-prd or above includes the needed action.
The request is allowed, because Contributor is a broad role that covers all resource groups in the subscription.
The request is allowed, because the contractor's role in rg-sap-dev is added to whatever exists in rg-sap-prd.
The request is refused only if the contractor also lacks a password, since Azure checks the password first.
questions.why: Azure asks whether any assignment at the target's scope or above includes the action, and a grant at rg-sap-dev does not reach the sibling resource group rg-sap-prd.

questions.prompt: An administrator grants a group the Contributor role at the management group mg-corp-all to speed up onboarding. Which statement describes the effect of this grant?
choices: It applies only to the first subscription the administrator selects, chosen when the grant is made.
It flows down to every subscription, resource group, and resource beneath mg-corp-all, which is why the grant is risky.
It applies only to resources the group creates after the grant, not to those that already exist.
It applies only to the management group object itself and not to any subscriptions beneath it.
questions.why: A grant at a higher scope flows down to everything beneath it, so a broad role at a management group reaches all of its subscriptions and their resources.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide what Azure access a new SAP operations engineer should receive. Name the scope you would start at, and state one limit or tradeoff of that choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start at the resource group that holds the SAP systems the engineer will operate, not the subscription. I would assign a built-in role that covers only the actions their tasks need, such as restarting virtual machines, and I would give that role to a group rather than to the person, so access can be changed in one place. The main tradeoff is that a resource group scope is narrower, so anything the engineer needs outside that group, such as shared network resources in another group, requires a separate, deliberate assignment. That extra step is slower, but it stops access spreading quietly through inheritance. SAP-level permissions still need their own review, because Azure roles do not control what a user can do inside the SAP application.
rubricPoints: Starts at the narrowest scope that covers the needed resources, such as a resource group, not the subscription.
Grants the least-privileged role and assigns it to a group, not to individuals.
Names a tradeoff: narrow scopes need extra assignments for resources outside the group.
Notes that Azure RBAC does not control permissions inside the SAP application.

suggested.rationale: A planned authorization policy evaluator would let learners test which role assignments allow or refuse a request at each scope, which is the core reasoning this objective needs.

lessons.plain: Azure Policy is a rules engine for your cloud accounts. You write a rule such as 'virtual machines must be in one approved region' or 'every resource must carry a cost-center tag', attach it to a part of your organisation, and the platform checks new and existing resources against it. Some rules block a change before it happens, some only report that something is out of line, and some can fix settings automatically. For an SAP landscape, this is how a team keeps production systems in approved regions and sizes without relying on people remembering a checklist.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your company wants every new server in an SAP landscape to be in one approved region. Would you rather block non-compliant servers at the moment they are created, or only get a report afterward? What does each choice cost you?
lessons.teach:
A policy definition is one rule: a condition that matches resources (for example, the resource type is a virtual machine and its location is not on an approved list) plus an effect that says what happens when it matches. A policy assignment attaches a definition to a scope, which is a management group, a subscription, or a resource group. Resources inside that scope inherit the assignment, so a rule set high in the hierarchy covers everything below it. An initiative, also called a policy set, bundles several definitions so they can be assigned and reported on together, such as a regulated-industry baseline for an SAP estate.

Why it works: the platform evaluates each condition against a resource's properties when it is created or changed, and also in the background against resources that already exist, recording compliance per resource. The effect decides the response. Deny blocks the request. Audit lets the request through and marks the resource non-compliant. Modify and deployIfNotExists add or change settings, which suits tags or diagnostic settings.

Worked example: an assignment on the SAP production subscription uses Deny for locations outside an approved region. An engineer submits a VM deployment in a different region. Step 1: the request is evaluated against the assignment. Step 2: the location is off the approved list, so Deny rejects the request before anything is created. Step 3: the same VM submitted in the approved region is accepted.

Common mistake: expecting Deny to clean up what already exists. Deny acts only on new or changed resources. Audit reports existing non-compliant resources, and modify or deployIfNotExists fix existing ones only when a remediation task is run.

Consequence: a Deny rule assigned too high in the hierarchy can block an unrelated workload, and a pipeline that fails on a policy rejection can look like a platform fault until someone reads the policy result.
