questions.prompt: A logistics company assigns an initiative to the resource group rg-erp-qas, using the Audit effect for storage accounts that allow public network access. Audit lets requests through and marks a matching resource non-compliant. An existing storage account, stqasbackup, was created before the assignment and already allows public access. Step 1: the platform evaluates stqasbackup in the background against the assignment. Step 2: the platform records stqasbackup as non-compliant. Complete step 3 with the one action that follows from the Audit effect.
choices: The account keeps running unchanged and stays marked non-compliant until someone changes its setting.
Deny deletes stqasbackup because it breaks the rule.
The team is blocked from reading stqasbackup until the setting is fixed.
Audit switches public access off on stqasbackup automatically.
questions.why: Audit neither blocks nor changes existing resources; it only records them as non-compliant, so the account continues as it was until someone corrects it.

questions.prompt: A retail chain has 14 subscriptions under one management group and wants a single rule to apply to all of them. Where should the policy assignment be made?
choices: One assignment at the management group scope, inherited by the subscriptions below it
A bundled initiative kept in one subscription, which covers every other subscription automatically
A policy definition on each subscription, since definitions cannot be inherited
An assignment at each of the 14 resource groups
questions.why: An assignment at a management group scope passes down to every subscription and resource beneath it, so one assignment covers all 14 subscriptions.

questions.prompt: A pipeline deploying a database server to an SAP subscription fails with a rejection that mentions a policy. Which step should the engineer take first?
choices: Remove the Deny effect from the subscription so the pipeline passes
Run a remediation task, which will undo the rejection
Assume the platform is faulty and restart the deployment agent
Read the policy evaluation result to see which assignment and effect rejected the request
questions.why: The policy result names the assignment and effect that rejected the request, which is the fastest way to tell a policy block from a platform fault.

questions.prompt: A finance team wants every new resource in its six resource groups to receive a cost-center tag automatically when it is created. Which effect fits this need?
choices: Deny, since it adds missing tags before the resource is created
Audit, since it writes the missing tag onto the resource
Deny, since it rejects the request and marks the resource non-compliant
Modify, since it adds or changes settings such as tags
questions.why: Modify is the effect meant for adding or changing settings such as tags, whereas Deny only blocks requests and Audit only reports them.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how Azure Policy decides what happens to a deployment that breaks a rule, and name one limit or tradeoff of putting a Deny rule at a management group.
lessons.modelAnswer: Azure Policy checks a rule against a resource when that resource is created or changed. The assignment's effect decides the outcome. Deny rejects the request. Audit allows it but records the resource as non-compliant. Modify and deployIfNotExists can add or change settings. Existing resources are not blocked by Deny; they only appear in the compliance report, and a remediation task is needed to fix them with the automated effects. The main tradeoff of assigning Deny at a management group is reach. The rule applies to every subscription beneath it, so a rule written for the SAP production estate can also block a sandbox or a shared network deployment that nobody meant to restrict. A sensible approach is to run the rule as Audit first, check the compliance results, and only then move it to Deny at the right scope.
rubricPoints: Explains that the effect (Deny, Audit, modify, deployIfNotExists) determines the outcome
States that Deny acts on new or changed resources, while existing ones need reporting or remediation
Describes assignment scope and inheritance down the management group, subscription, and resource group hierarchy
Names a concrete tradeoff of broad-scope Deny rules, such as blocking unrelated workloads

suggested.rationale: Choosing between Deny, Audit, and remediation at a given scope is best practised by reasoning through a realistic governance scenario.

lessons.plain: Authentication is the step where a system checks that someone or something is who it claims to be, usually by asking for a password, a certificate, or a signed token issued by a trusted directory. SAP workloads run business software that many people and background programs use, so this step decides who gets through the front door at all. Designing it means choosing where identities live, such as a central company directory, how people sign in once and reach several SAP systems, and how automated programs prove themselves without passwords stored in scripts. Authentication is separate from authorization, which decides what a person may do after they are inside. A good design answers two questions: where is the proof checked, and what happens when that checker is unavailable.
lessons.guessPrompt: A finance clerk signs into an SAP system on Monday and then has to sign in again to each of four other SAP systems during the same morning. What would you change first to reduce the repeated sign-ins, and why might that change still carry a risk you would need to manage?
lessons.teach:
An identity provider is a service that stores user accounts and checks passwords or other proof on behalf of other systems. Single sign-on (SSO) means a user proves who they are once, and other systems accept that proof without asking again. Federation is the arrangement where an SAP system trusts an identity provider it does not run itself. The proof passed between them is usually a signed token, a short piece of data that the identity provider signs with a private key so the SAP system can verify it with a matching public certificate. A service account is an identity used by a program rather than a person, and a managed identity is an Azure-issued identity for a cloud resource that avoids storing a password at all.

Why it works: one trusted source of identities means one place to disable someone who leaves, and one place to enforce multi-factor checks. Worked example, step by step. First, Ana signs in to the company directory, Microsoft Entra ID, with her password and a second factor. Second, the directory issues a signed assertion saying this is Ana, valid for a few minutes. Third, the SAP system checks the signature against the directory certificate it trusts, checks the expiry time, and maps the name to an SAP user. Fourth, SAP opens a session. Authorization roles then decide what she can do.

Common mistake: treating a successful sign-in as permission, or leaving local SAP passwords enabled for ordinary users so that the central control is quietly bypassed. Background jobs also get mistaken for people, and their passwords end up in scripts. Consequence in a running system: if the directory is unreachable or a signing certificate expires, nobody can sign in at all, so a sound design includes break-glass accounts and alerts before certificates lapse.

questions.prompt: Northgate Foods runs a nightly stock report on an Azure virtual machine. The report program is a background job, so it uses the VM's managed identity rather than a password stored in its script. Here is the flow for that job, with one step left out. 1. The job asks Azure for a token on behalf of the VM's managed identity, and no password is stored anywhere. 2. The identity platform issues a signed token for that identity, valid for a short window. 3. [missing step] 4. SAP opens a session for the mapped service user, and that user's roles allow only reading stock tables. Which statement fills the missing step?
choices: SAP asks the VM's administrator to type a password before it accepts the job's request.
SAP checks the token's signature against the trusted certificate and checks its expiry time, then maps the identity to an SAP user.
The job writes the token into its log file so that the nightly run can be audited later.
SAP skips all checks because the VM sits on the internal virtual network and so is already trusted.
questions.why: Before SAP maps the identity and opens a session, it must verify the token's signature against a certificate it trusts and confirm the token has not expired, which is the check that makes a signed token worth accepting.

questions.prompt: In plain terms, what does federation mean in the context of an SAP system?
choices: Several SAP systems share one database so that each one can read the same user list.
Users are given the same password on every SAP system so they can switch between them without signing in again.
The SAP system trusts an identity provider it does not run itself and accepts signed proof from that provider.
The SAP system stores every user's password in its own local table so that sign-ins never depend on another service.
questions.why: Federation is the arrangement in which an SAP system trusts an external identity provider and accepts the signed proof that provider issues, instead of managing those identities itself.

questions.prompt: A company's token-signing certificate, which its SAP systems use to verify sign-in proof, expires on a Friday evening, and nobody has renewed it. What is the most likely result for ordinary users on Monday morning?
choices: Users cannot sign in through the central directory, because the SAP systems can no longer verify the signed proof.
Only users with the SAP_ALL role are locked out, while everyone else keeps full access.
Sign-ins keep working, because the SAP systems cache earlier tokens indefinitely.
Users can still sign in with the local SAP passwords, so nothing visible changes.
questions.why: When the certificate that verifies signed tokens lapses, the SAP systems can no longer confirm the proof, so federated sign-ins fail for everyone, which is why certificate expiry needs alerts well before it happens.

questions.prompt: A nightly interface program must call an SAP system without a person being present. Which identity arrangement fits this requirement best?
choices: A shared account named after the department, with its password pasted into the program's configuration file.
The personal account of the senior developer who wrote the program, so that the calls are traced to a real person.
A service account or managed identity for the program, with its roles limited to what the interface needs and no password stored in the script.
A single administrator account that already has every role, so that no permission changes are ever needed.
questions.why: A program running without a person should use a service account or managed identity with narrow roles and no password in scripts, because a personal or shared login would mix program activity with people and leak credentials.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a user signs into an SAP system through a central identity provider, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying on a single identity provider.
lessons.modelAnswer: The user signs in once to the central directory, usually with a password plus a second factor. The directory issues a short-lived signed token that states who the user is. The SAP system checks that token's signature against a certificate it already trusts and checks its expiry, then maps the identity to an SAP user and opens a session. Roles inside SAP still decide what the user can do, so sign-in and permission are separate steps. The main tradeoff is dependency: if the identity provider is down or a signing certificate expires, nobody can sign in, so the design needs break-glass accounts, monitoring of certificate expiry, and a documented fallback. Background programs should use service identities or managed identities rather than shared passwords, since they cannot complete an interactive sign-in.
rubricPoints: Describes the central identity provider issuing a signed, short-lived token that the SAP system verifies.
Separates authentication (who you are) from authorization (what you may do).
Names a real limit, such as an outage or expired certificate blocking all sign-ins.
Notes that background programs need service or managed identities, not shared passwords.

suggested.rationale: Explaining the sign-in chain and its failure modes back to a teammate is the core skill here, and no listed mission teaches it directly.

lessons.plain: When a cloud-hosted SAP application asks who you are, it often does not keep its own password list. Instead it sends you to a separate trusted service, called an identity provider, which verifies you and then vouches for you back to the application. This is called single sign-on, because one sign-in works across several applications. Designing authentication means deciding which identity service is the source of truth, how the application trusts its answers, how user accounts are created and removed automatically, and which extra checks, such as a second proof of identity, apply. Getting these choices right keeps access both safe and easy to withdraw when someone leaves.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company wants its SAP cloud application to use the same sign-in as its email and other office apps. Without any technical background, what do you think should hold the passwords, and what should happen to the app's access when an employee leaves?
lessons.teach:
Authentication means proving who a user is. Authorization, a separate question, decides what that proven user may do, and is taught in another objective. Federation means the application trusts a separate identity provider, which is the service that holds user accounts and checks passwords. Two common trust formats are SAML, which exchanges signed XML documents called assertions, and OpenID Connect, which is a sign-in layer built on OAuth 2.0 and returns signed tokens. A claim is a piece of information inside such an assertion or token, such as the user's name or group membership. Provisioning means creating, updating and removing matching accounts in the application, often automated with SCIM, a standard protocol for account management. Multi-factor authentication (MFA) requires a second proof, such as an approval on a phone, in addition to the password. A break-glass account is a tightly controlled emergency administrator account used only when the normal sign-in path fails.

Why it works: the application never receives the user's password. It trusts the identity provider because each assertion or token is signed with a key the application already knows. Before starting a session, the application checks the signature, that the message was meant for it, and that it has not expired. Disabling the account in the identity provider then blocks new sign-ins everywhere that account is federated.

Worked example. A contractor opens the application's address. Step 1: the application finds no session and redirects the browser to the identity provider. Step 2: the contractor signs in and passes MFA. Step 3: the provider issues a signed assertion naming the user and a group claim, such as finance-readers. Step 4: the application verifies the signature and audience, then maps that group to an application role. Step 5: when the contract ends, the provider disables the account, and the next sign-in attempt fails.

Common mistake: leaving a local fallback password enabled inside the application 'just in case'. Anyone who knows that path bypasses MFA and the provider's sign-in policies entirely.

Consequence in a running system: if the identity provider has an outage or a misconfigured sign-in policy, every federated user is locked out at once. Good designs therefore keep a tested, monitored break-glass path for administrators, and treat the identity provider as critical infrastructure.

questions.prompt: A logistics company's supplier portal uses OpenID Connect with an external identity provider. A supplier named Harbor Freight Co-op signs in and passes MFA. The steps so far: (1) the portal finds no session and redirects the browser to the identity provider; (2) the supplier signs in and completes MFA; (3) the provider returns a signed token containing a claim department=procurement and an audience value naming the portal. Step 4 is missing. Before the portal starts a session for this supplier, what must it do with the token?
choices: Send the department claim to a SCIM endpoint to create the account
Create a local fallback password so the supplier can sign in if the provider fails later
Verify the token's signature, confirm the audience names this portal, and check the token has not expired
Copy the supplier's password from the token into the portal's own user table
questions.why: The application must check the signature, that the token was meant for it, and that it has not expired before it trusts the token and starts a session.

questions.prompt: In the teaching sense, what does provisioning mean?
choices: Proving a user's identity with a password and a second factor
Deciding which actions a signed-in user is allowed to perform
Creating, updating and removing matching accounts in the application
Redirecting a browser to a separate identity provider when no session exists
questions.why: Provisioning is the account lifecycle work of creating, updating and removing matching accounts in the application, often automated with SCIM.

questions.prompt: A SaaS application receives a sign-in assertion whose signature cannot be verified with any key the application already knows. What should the application do?
choices: Ask the user for their password and trust the assertion after that
Accept the assertion, because the user's name and group claim are present
Store the assertion and retry verification later without blocking the sign-in
Reject the assertion, because the application relies on the signature to trust the identity provider
questions.why: Trust in federation rests on the signature being checked against a key the application knows, so an assertion that fails that check must be refused.

questions.prompt: A company keeps a local fallback password enabled inside its federated application 'just in case' the identity provider fails. What is the main risk of this choice?
choices: The application can no longer read group claims from assertions
Provisioning through SCIM will stop working for all accounts
Users will need to remember two passwords, which slows sign-in
Anyone who knows that path can sign in without the provider's MFA and sign-in policies
questions.why: A local password path bypasses the provider's MFA and sign-in policies, which is the weakness the teaching text warns about.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a user signs in to a federated SAP SaaS application, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying on a single identity provider.
lessons.modelAnswer: I'd describe it as a handoff. The SaaS app doesn't check the user's password itself. It redirects the browser to our identity provider, which checks the password and any MFA prompt. The provider then sends back a signed statement saying who the user is and which groups they belong to. The app checks the signature and that the statement was meant for it, then opens a session and maps the groups to roles. The tradeoff is that the identity provider becomes a single dependency. If it is down or a sign-in policy is misconfigured, nobody can sign in to any federated app, so we need a tested break-glass admin path and monitoring on the provider. Groups that feed role mapping also have to be kept clean, or stale access lingers after people change jobs.
rubricPoints: Describes the redirect to the identity provider, which verifies the user rather than the SaaS app checking passwords itself
Explains that the app trusts a signed assertion or token and checks its signature, audience and expiry
Names a tradeoff such as the identity provider being a single point of failure or lockout risk
Mentions a safeguard such as a tested break-glass path, MFA, or removing local fallback passwords

suggested.rationale: Choosing between federation, provisioning and MFA for a given SaaS scenario is an exam-style reasoning task, and no listed mission covers identity federation.

lessons.plain: Think of a large company that owns many buildings, each with rooms and furniture. A management hierarchy is the way a cloud account is arranged into layers so that rules, access and bills can be applied at the right level. At the top sits a broad grouping that can hold rules for many projects. Below it sit separate billing and quota boundaries called subscriptions. Inside those sit folders called resource groups that hold the individual servers, disks and networks that belong together. For SAP landscapes this matters because one rule set can cover every production system while test systems stay separate. Getting these layers right early saves painful moves later.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose your company runs three SAP systems (development, quality test and production), and a security rule says all production systems must be encrypted. Where would you prefer to attach that rule so it reaches production but not development: on each server one by one, on one shared folder, or on a grouping that contains only the production boundary? Explain your choice in a sentence.
lessons.teach:
A management hierarchy is the layered structure that organises everything in a cloud account. Three layers matter here. A management group is a container for subscriptions; rules and access assignments placed on it flow down to everything beneath it. A subscription is a billing and quota boundary: its invoice, its spending and its resource limits (quotas) are tracked separately. A resource group is a folder inside a subscription that holds resources sharing a lifecycle, such as the virtual machines, disks and network interfaces of one SAP system.

Why it works: rules are inherited downward. Assign something once high up and it applies to every child without repeating the work, while a rule placed low only affects that branch. This lets you separate concerns: governance at the top, cost and quota per subscription, and day-to-day grouping per resource group.

Worked example. Step 1: a management group called SAP-Production contains a subscription called SAP-PRD-Core. Step 2: a rule requiring disk encryption is assigned to SAP-Production. Step 3: a new resource group called rg-hana-prd is created inside SAP-PRD-Core. Step 4: a database server deployed into rg-hana-prd is evaluated and inherits the rule automatically. Step 5: a development subscription under a separate management group never receives the rule, so its tests stay unaffected.

Common mistake: treating the resource group as a security or billing boundary. A resource group is not the usual unit for quota or spend limits, and moving a resource to another group can change which rules apply to it. Subscriptions are the usual unit for quota and spend.

Consequence in a running system: a subscription placed in the wrong branch of the hierarchy can silently miss a required rule, so production systems may run without the controls an audit expects.

questions.prompt: Northwind Logistics has a management group called Retail-Prod with a rule that allows deployments only in two approved regions. A new subscription called NW-SAP-QAS is needed for SAP quality testing. Step 1: NW-SAP-QAS is created and placed under a management group called Retail-Dev, which has no regional rule. Step 2: a resource group called rg-sap-qas-app is created inside NW-SAP-QAS. Step 3: a VM is deployed into rg-sap-qas-app in an unapproved region and is allowed, because nothing above it blocks the deployment. Step 4: [missing step]. Result: from now on, a VM deployed into rg-sap-qas-app in an unapproved region is blocked by the regional rule.
choices: Tag rg-sap-qas-app with the name of the approved region so that the rule can find the resources it governs.
Delete rg-sap-qas-app and recreate it, because a resource group keeps only the rules that were present when it was created.
Create a spending limit on rg-sap-qas-app, because spending limits are the mechanism that enforces regional rules.
Move NW-SAP-QAS under Retail-Prod so the regional rule flows down to it and to everything beneath it.
questions.why: Rules are inherited downward from the management group where they are placed, so the subscription must sit under Retail-Prod for the regional rule to reach it and its resource groups.

questions.prompt: In a management hierarchy, which layer is the usual unit for setting spend limits and resource quotas?
choices: The network interface attached to a database server
The resource group that holds the VMs and disks of one SAP system
The management group placed directly above the subscriptions
The subscription, because its invoice, spending and quotas are tracked separately
questions.why: A subscription is the billing and quota boundary, so its spending and resource limits are tracked and set at that level rather than at a folder or container above or below it.

questions.prompt: Contoso's management group Lab-Tree has no regional or encryption rule. Its sandbox subscription SBX-01 sits there. A rule requiring disk encryption is assigned to Corp-Prod, a separate management group in a different branch. A team then creates a VM in a resource group inside SBX-01. Does the encryption rule apply to that VM?
choices: Yes, because the resource group is the point where rules are inherited from the hierarchy
Yes, because rules assigned anywhere in the account apply to every resource in every subscription
No, because the rule was assigned to a different branch and only flows downward from the point where it is placed
Only if the VM is given a tag that repeats the name of the encryption rule
questions.why: Inheritance flows downward only, so a rule on a sibling branch never reaches a subscription that sits elsewhere in the hierarchy.

questions.prompt: Tailspin Traders wants a monthly spending cap for its SAP development work. The team sets the cap on a resource group called rg-tt-dev-sap, which lives inside the subscription TT-SAP-Dev. What is the main problem with this setup?
choices: The cap will only begin to count spending after the next restart of the virtual machines
Resource groups hold no billing data, so the cap should be placed on each VM individually
Resource groups are not the usual unit for spend and quota, so the cap belongs on the subscription TT-SAP-Dev
Spending caps cannot be set at any level below a management group, so the cap was never valid
questions.why: Spend and quota are tracked per subscription, so a cap on a resource group is the wrong boundary and would not reflect the subscription's true billing.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would arrange management groups, subscriptions and resource groups for an SAP landscape with development, test and production systems, and name one limit or tradeoff of the layout you choose.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would place production and non-production subscriptions under separate management groups, so governance rules such as required encryption or allowed regions apply to production from the top without touching sandboxes. Within each environment I would use one subscription per landscape tier, because the subscription is where spending and quota are tracked and where a team can be given its own limits. Inside a subscription, resource groups would follow the SAP system boundary: one group per system, holding its database, application servers, disks and network pieces, so they can be reviewed, tagged and deleted together. The tradeoff is more subscriptions to manage and more quota requests to track. A shared network used by several systems may also need its own resource group that does not match any single system. Finally, moving a resource later can change which rules apply to it, so the layout should be settled before deployment.
rubricPoints: Management groups carry governance rules that inherit down to subscriptions and their resources.
Subscriptions are the boundary for billing, spending and quota limits.
Resource groups group resources that share a lifecycle, such as one SAP system.
A tradeoff exists: more subscriptions mean more management and quota overhead, and shared resources may not fit one system's group.
Moving resources between groups can change which rules apply.

suggested.rationale: Designing a hierarchy is best checked by the learner explaining the layout and its tradeoffs, since no listed mission or engine covers this topic directly.

lessons.plain: A landing zone is the prepared foundation you build in a cloud account before any real systems arrive. Think of it as laying the floors, wiring, locks and address labels in a new building before moving the furniture in. For SAP, that foundation decides how environments are separated, how they reach your office network, who may administer them, and which rules are enforced automatically. Getting it right first means every SAP system that follows inherits sound security and networking instead of each team inventing its own.
lessons.guessPrompt: If your company is about to host separate SAP development, test and production systems in the cloud, what would you set up first, before installing any SAP system, and why?
lessons.teach:
A landing zone is a repeatable set of cloud foundations: containers for resources, a network design, identity and access rules, and governance policies. In Azure, the main account boundary is the subscription, a container for billing and access. A management group is a container that groups subscriptions so that a rule applied once flows down to all of them. A resource group is a folder inside a subscription that holds related resources, such as the virtual machines for one SAP system. A virtual network is a private, isolated network in the cloud, and a hub-and-spoke design places shared connections in one central network (the hub) and workload networks (spokes) that connect to it.

Why it works: boundaries are cheap to draw early and expensive to redraw later. Separating production from non-production at the subscription level means a risky change in development cannot touch production permissions or spending. A policy that restricts approved regions can be assigned once at the management group level and applies everywhere below it. With SAP RISE, SAP operates the systems in its own environment, so your landing zone concentrates on the connections and identity links to it.

Worked example. A company runs SAP development, quality and production. Step 1: create a management group for SAP and place one subscription under it for each environment. Step 2: assign a policy at that group allowing only approved regions, which now covers all three subscriptions. Step 3: build a hub network holding the link to the corporate network and a firewall. Step 4: give each environment a spoke network with its own address range, and peer each spoke to the hub. Step 5: grant production administrators rights only on the production subscription.

Common mistake: giving every SAP environment the same private address range to keep things simple. Later connections fail because routes collide, and fixing it means redeploying the systems.

In a running landscape, a network design that cannot be connected is an outage waiting to happen, so the address plan is one of the first decisions to make.

questions.prompt: Brightwater Logistics, a firm that runs SAP for three of its sites, wants an outside SAP consultant to work only in the sandbox subscription. The sequence is: Step 1: confirm the consultant needs the sandbox and nothing else. Step 2: create a role assignment scoped to the sandbox subscription. Step 3: missing. Step 4: have the consultant sign in and confirm that the production subscription shows no access. Which action fills Step 3?
choices: Remove or narrow the consultant's older broad rights that were inherited from the management group above the sandbox, so they no longer flow down to production.
Place the consultant's sandbox in its own hub network so that its routes are kept separate.
Grant the consultant contributor rights at the management group so they can move resources between environments.
Assign a policy that restricts the sandbox to a single region.
questions.why: Rights assigned high in the hierarchy flow down to every subscription beneath, so the broad inherited rights must be removed or narrowed before the scoped assignment can guarantee no production access.

questions.prompt: In an Azure landing zone, what is a management group?
choices: A private network that links an SAP hub to its spoke networks.
A folder inside a subscription that holds the virtual machines for one SAP system.
A billing record that tracks how much each SAP environment spends each month.
A container that groups subscriptions so that a rule applied once flows down to all of them.
questions.why: The teaching text defines a management group as a container that groups subscriptions so a rule applied at that level reaches every subscription below it.

questions.prompt: A company has four SAP systems in one subscription and plans to add two more subscriptions next quarter. It wants a rule that allows only approved regions to apply to all six. Where should the rule be assigned?
choices: On the virtual machine of each SAP system.
On the hub network only, since it is the one shared network.
On a management group that contains all the subscriptions that will hold these systems.
On each individual resource group as the systems are deployed.
questions.why: A rule assigned at a management group flows down to every subscription beneath it, including ones added later, so it covers all six without repeated setup.

questions.prompt: Two spoke networks are each given the address range 10.0.0.0/16, and both try to peer with the same hub. Why is this a serious problem in a running landscape?
choices: The hub can only accept spokes that use a range larger than /16.
Overlapping address ranges make routes ambiguous, so connections fail and fixing it means redeploying the systems.
Spoke networks are not allowed to use private address ranges at all.
The subscription's billing is split between the two spokes, which blocks the peering.
questions.why: When two networks claim the same addresses, traffic cannot be routed unambiguously, which breaks connections and usually forces a redeployment to change the address plan.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would structure an Azure landing zone for separate SAP development and production environments. Name one limit or tradeoff of your design.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would give each environment its own subscription, and group those subscriptions under one SAP management group. That lets me assign a policy once, such as allowed regions or required tags, and have it apply to both. Production gets its own spoke network connected to a shared hub that holds the link to our corporate network and the firewall. Each spoke gets a distinct address range so the peering works, and production admin rights stay on the production subscription only. The tradeoff is overhead: separate subscriptions mean more to manage, more cost tracking and more role assignments, and the hub becomes a shared dependency that needs careful change control.
rubricPoints: Separates environments with subscriptions or similar boundaries, not just resource groups
Uses management groups so policies and rules apply to many subscriptions at once
Plans non-overlapping network address ranges and a hub or shared connectivity point
Names a real tradeoff, such as added administrative overhead or a shared hub as a dependency

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine covers landing zone design, and the core skill is explaining a structure and its tradeoffs back in your own words.

lessons.plain: RISE with SAP is a service where SAP runs your SAP systems for you, and the servers sit inside a network that SAP manages on Azure. Your company still has its own network, offices, and users, so the two networks have to reach each other safely. Designing the networking means deciding how your network connects to SAP's, which address ranges each side uses, how names get resolved, and which traffic is allowed through. Get it wrong and users cannot reach their SAP system, or the two networks collide on the same addresses without anyone noticing.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your company network uses the address range 10.1.0.0/16, and the managed SAP network also uses 10.1.0.0/16. Before reading any further, what do you think goes wrong when you try to connect the two?
lessons.teach:
Definitions. A virtual network is a private address space in the cloud that you divide into smaller ranges called subnets. RISE with SAP is SAP's managed offering in which SAP operates the SAP landscape, and in this course its infrastructure sits in an Azure network that SAP runs. Your organization keeps its own network, so the design task is the connection between the two. A site-to-site VPN sends encrypted traffic across the internet between two networks. ExpressRoute is a private, dedicated circuit obtained from a connectivity provider, and it avoids the public internet. Peering links two virtual networks so they route to each other directly. A hub-and-spoke design places shared connectivity, such as gateways and firewalls, in a hub network, with workloads in spoke networks that connect through it.

Why it works. A router forwards each packet by looking at its destination address. If both sides claim the same range, the router cannot tell which side a packet belongs to, so traffic goes to the wrong place or nowhere. Name resolution must also work: SAP host names have to resolve from your side through DNS, or applications connect to the wrong address or fail to connect at all.

Worked example. Suppose your corporate network uses 10.20.0.0/16 and SAP's managed network uses 10.50.0.0/16. Step 1: confirm the two ranges do not overlap. Step 2: establish a VPN or ExpressRoute link with routes exchanged in both directions. Step 3: open only the SAP ports your users and interfaces need, limited to the source ranges that need them. Step 4: configure DNS forwarding so SAP host names resolve from your side. Step 5: test a real login from an office client.

Common mistake. Choosing a convenient range such as 10.0.0.0/16 on your side without checking the range assigned to the SAP network, then finding the overlap only after cutover.

Consequence. Overlapping ranges and missing routes usually show up as timeouts that affect only some networks. These are slow to diagnose once production traffic depends on the connection.

questions.prompt: A manufacturer's office network uses 172.16.0.0/14 and its SAP RISE network uses 10.80.0.0/16, so the ranges do not overlap. The team did the following: (1) confirmed the ranges do not overlap; (2) set up an ExpressRoute circuit, a private dedicated link from a connectivity provider, with routes exchanged in both directions; (3) opened only the SAP ports needed from the office subnets; (5) logged in from an office laptop using an SAP host name, and the login succeeded. Later, a colleague found that a different office could reach the SAP systems only by typing raw IP addresses, and every host-name lookup failed there. The step the team skipped is the one that makes SAP host names resolve from the office side. What is that missing step?
choices: Renumber the office network to a range that is smaller than the SAP network
Add a site-to-site VPN as a backup path over the public internet
Configure DNS forwarding so SAP host names resolve from the office networks through DNS
Create a hub-and-spoke layout with the firewall placed in the SAP network
questions.why: Name resolution through DNS must be configured separately from routing, so host names only resolve on the office side once DNS forwarding is set up.

questions.prompt: A retail chain wants its warehouse network to reach its SAP RISE landscape through a private, dedicated link that avoids the public internet. Which connection type fits this requirement?
choices: Network peering, because it links two virtual networks directly
ExpressRoute, because it is a private circuit from a connectivity provider
A hub-and-spoke design, because it places gateways in a central network
A site-to-site VPN, because it encrypts traffic across the internet
questions.why: ExpressRoute is the private dedicated circuit option, while a VPN still crosses the public internet and peering only joins two virtual networks inside the cloud.

questions.prompt: A logistics company's corporate network uses 10.0.0.0/16, and its SAP RISE network uses 10.0.128.0/17. Users report that some connections time out, but only from certain office networks. What is the most likely root cause?
choices: The SAP ports are closed for all source ranges
The two address ranges overlap, so routers cannot tell which side a packet belongs to
The VPN encryption is too weak for the traffic volume
DNS forwarding was turned off for the SAP host names
questions.why: 10.0.128.0/17 sits inside 10.0.0.0/16, so the ranges overlap, and overlapping ranges cause routing confusion that shows up as partial timeouts.

questions.prompt: A company has three spoke virtual networks that each need to reach SAP RISE through a shared firewall and gateway. Where should the shared firewall and gateway be placed in a hub-and-spoke design?
choices: In the SAP RISE network, so SAP operates the firewall
In each spoke, so every workload has its own copy
In a central hub network, with the spokes connecting through it
In the public internet edge, outside any virtual network
questions.why: In a hub-and-spoke design, shared connectivity such as gateways and firewalls sits in the hub, and the spoke workloads connect through it.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why the address ranges of your network and the RISE managed network must not overlap, and name one tradeoff between a site-to-site VPN and ExpressRoute for this connection.
lessons.modelAnswer: Routing works by matching each packet's destination address to exactly one network. If your network and the RISE managed network both use the same range, the routers cannot tell which side a packet belongs to, so some traffic goes to the wrong place or fails silently. We need to check the ranges before we connect anything, and that check usually has to happen before cutover, because changing an address range later is disruptive. For the link itself, a site-to-site VPN is quicker to set up and cheaper, but it runs over the public internet, so latency and bandwidth vary. ExpressRoute is a private circuit with more predictable performance, but it takes longer to provision and costs more. For a production SAP landscape where response time matters, that tradeoff is what we should weigh and document.
rubricPoints: Overlapping address ranges make routing ambiguous, so the ranges must be checked and kept distinct before connecting.
A VPN is quicker and cheaper but crosses the public internet, while ExpressRoute is private and more predictable but slower and costlier to provision.
DNS must resolve SAP host names from the customer side, or applications fail even when routes exist.
Firewall rules should allow only the SAP ports and source ranges that are actually needed.

suggested.rationale: Tracing how a packet travels between two networks, and where it would be blocked or misrouted, is the reasoning this objective requires and the planned virtual network path tracer would practise it.

lessons.plain: SAP RISE is a way of buying SAP software where a provider runs the SAP system for you in a cloud environment it manages. Your company still has its own office network, data centre, and users, so those networks have to reach the SAP environment privately. Networking here means building a secure path between your network and the SAP environment, deciding which private addresses each side uses, making names resolve, and agreeing who controls which firewall rules. If the path is missing or badly planned, users cannot log on even though the SAP system itself is healthy.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your company's own network uses the private address block 10.1.0.0/16. The SAP RISE environment also uses 10.1.0.0/16. Can users reach the SAP system over a private link as it stands? What would you change, and why?
lessons.teach:
A virtual network is a private, isolated network inside a cloud subscription, with its own address range. A /16 range is a block of 65,536 private addresses. In a SAP RISE setup, the SAP landscape sits in a virtual network managed by the provider, and your company needs a private link into it. Common link types are a site-to-site VPN, which encrypts traffic over the internet, and a dedicated private circuit such as ExpressRoute, a leased connection that does not cross the public internet. Either way, the link only carries packets; it does not decide who may talk to whom.

Three things must line up. First, address ranges must not overlap, because if both sides use the same block, a router cannot tell which side a packet belongs to. Second, routes must be correct on both sides, so traffic to and from the SAP range goes through the link and replies come back the same way. Third, name resolution must work: SAP clients find application servers by name through DNS, the system that translates names to addresses, so each side must be able to answer for the other's names.

Worked example. Your corporate network uses 10.1.0.0/16 and the RISE landscape also uses 10.1.0.0/16. Step 1: compare the ranges and see that they overlap completely. Step 2: agree a non-overlapping range for the SAP side, such as 10.50.0.0/20, and have the provider reconfigure. Step 3: add routes for the new range on both sides. Step 4: confirm DNS resolves SAP host names from your users' network. Step 5: test a logon from a client machine.

Common mistake: assuming a NAT device, which rewrites addresses, will hide the overlap. It may work for one path but breaks as soon as a second network connects.

Consequence: with an overlap or a missing route, SAP GUI, the desktop client users log on with, times out while the SAP system runs normally. That looks like an SAP outage but is a network fault.

questions.prompt: Tidewater Insurance has a corporate network on 10.20.0.0/16 and proposes a RISE landscape on 10.20.128.0/18. Step 1: compare the two ranges and notice that 10.20.128.0/18 sits entirely inside 10.20.0.0/16, so they overlap. Step 2: ask the provider to move the SAP side to 10.90.0.0/19, which matches neither range. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: confirm that DNS on the corporate side resolves the SAP host names. Step 5: test a logon from a clinic-style desktop on the corporate network. What belongs in Step 3?
choices: Add routes for 10.90.0.0/19 on both the corporate and provider sides so traffic and replies use the link
Restart the SAP GUI clients on user desktops to clear cached addresses
Change the SAP subnet to a /16 so it is larger than the corporate range
Enable NAT on the corporate firewall so the old 10.20.128.0/18 addresses keep working
questions.why: Routes on both sides are what make traffic to and from the new SAP range go through the link and return the same way, which is the step that is missing here.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes what a site-to-site VPN or a dedicated private circuit such as ExpressRoute does in a SAP RISE setup?
choices: It rewrites addresses so that overlapping ranges are hidden from both networks
It is a leased circuit that replaces the need for DNS name resolution between the two sides
It encrypts all application traffic end to end, so access control between hosts is unnecessary
It carries packets between the networks but does not decide which hosts may talk to each other
questions.why: The teaching text states that the link only carries packets and does not decide who may talk to whom, so the answer is the one that says exactly that.

questions.prompt: Halvorsen Clinics has a working VPN to its provider's SAP landscape. The provider's monitoring shows the SAP application servers healthy, DNS resolves the SAP host names from clinic offices, and the provider has the clinic range in its routes. Yet SAP GUI logons from clinic desktops time out. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The SAP range is too large and must be split into smaller /24 subnets
A route for the SAP range is missing on the clinic side, so replies do not return through the link
The SAP application servers have crashed and need an immediate restart
The VPN must be replaced with ExpressRoute before any logon can succeed
questions.why: Healthy servers, working DNS and a route on one side point to a return-path routing fault on the other side, which the teaching text describes as a network fault that looks like an SAP outage.

questions.prompt: A corporate network uses 10.40.0.0/14, which covers addresses 10.40.0.0 through 10.43.255.255. Which proposed SAP range does not overlap with it?
questions.why: 10.44.0.0/20 begins just after the corporate block ends at 10.43.255.255, so no address is shared, while the other three each fall partly or wholly inside that block.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate who is new to cloud networking why overlapping address ranges stop a private link to a SAP RISE landscape from working, and what you would check before agreeing an address plan. Name one tradeoff in the fix you choose.
lessons.modelAnswer: Routers forward packets by destination address. If our corporate network and the SAP landscape both use 10.1.0.0/16, a router cannot tell whether a packet for 10.1.4.20 belongs to our office or to SAP, so traffic goes to the wrong side or nowhere. Before agreeing a plan, I would list every range in use on both sides, including future expansions, and confirm none overlap. I would also check the routes on both sides, that DNS resolves SAP names from our users' network, and that the firewall rules allow the SAP application ports. The fix is to ask the provider for a new non-overlapping range. The tradeoff is that it requires a change on the provider's side, so it takes coordination and time, and any hosts already configured with the old addresses need to be updated.
rubricPoints: Overlapping address ranges make routing ambiguous, so packets cannot reach the correct side.
A correct fix is a non-overlapping address plan agreed before connecting.
Routes and DNS on both sides must work for SAP names and traffic to resolve.
Firewall rules must allow the SAP application ports, and the link alone does not control access.
Changing the address range has a cost: provider coordination and reconfiguration.

suggested.rationale: Tracing the path between two address ranges and spotting where routes or overlaps break is exactly what the planned virtual network path tracer would practise.

lessons.plain: Imagine a company that wants SAP, its large business software, to run somewhere other than its own server room. SAP RISE is an arrangement where SAP itself runs and operates that software for the customer, while the cloud provider's servers, storage and networks sit underneath. Designing this on Azure means choosing the parts that hold the system: the virtual machines that act as servers, the private network that links them to the customer's offices, and the disks where the data lives. Each choice affects speed, cost, and who can reach what. This lesson is about naming which piece fits which requirement.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company's SAP system will run in the cloud, and its users sit in head office, connected to it by a private link. Before any teaching: which would you expect to control most directly whether users can reach the system and whether it is fast enough: the size of the virtual machines, the network design, or the disk type? Give your first guess and say why.
lessons.teach:
Three layers carry an SAP system on Azure. Compute means the virtual machines (VMs), which are rented servers with a set number of CPU cores and an amount of memory. SAP publishes which VM sizes it supports for its database and application servers, so the size is a supported-configuration decision, not only a cost decision. Network means the Azure virtual network, a private address range you divide into subnets, plus network security groups, which are allow and deny rules on traffic between subnets. Storage means managed disks attached to each VM, and for some large database layouts a shared file service that several servers can mount.

Why it is built this way: the application and database servers talk to each other constantly, so they belong in one virtual network with low delay between them. The customer's corporate network connects over a private link such as a VPN or ExpressRoute, so business traffic does not cross the public internet. Under RISE, SAP operates the landscape, so the customer's design work centres on the connections into it, identity, and the data placement the customer is responsible for.

Worked example: a company with about 1,000 users links its head office to a RISE landscape. Step 1: the database VM size is taken from the supported list. Step 2: the database data and log files go on premium disks with enough throughput for the workload. Step 3: the database subnet accepts traffic only from the application subnet on the database port. Step 4: the head office network is joined by a private link, and only the required routes are advertised. Each step maps to exactly one layer.

Common mistake: choosing a VM size from the price list alone, or opening the database subnet to the whole address range to make a connection work. The consequence is that an unsupported size can put the configuration outside what SAP supports, and an open subnet exposes the database to traffic it should never receive.

Every design question starts by deciding which layer a requirement belongs to, then which Azure component implements it.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm with about 800 users is moving its SAP landscape into a RISE arrangement. Its database has a large data volume that several database servers must mount at the same time. Step 1: the database VM size is taken from SAP's supported list for the planned core count. Step 2: [NOT GIVEN, the learner must choose the missing step]. Step 3: the corporate network is joined to the landscape over an ExpressRoute private link, and only the required routes are advertised. Which choice correctly completes Step 2?
choices: Attach a public IP address to each database VM so the shared volume can be reached from the office.
Put all data and log files on one large managed disk attached to the application server VM.
Move the database servers into the subnet that hosts the internet-facing gateway so that traffic has lower delay.
Place the shared data volume on a shared file service that the database servers mount, and keep the log files on managed disks attached to each VM.
questions.why: The shared file service is the storage component for a data layout that several servers must mount, while per-VM managed disks hold the log files, so option B is the storage decision that fits the requirement.

questions.prompt: In the Azure network layer, what does a network security group do?
choices: It divides the private address range into subnets and assigns each subnet a size.
It holds allow and deny rules that control which traffic may pass between subnets.
It rents the physical servers that run the SAP application and database tiers.
It provides the managed disks that are attached to each virtual machine.
questions.why: A network security group is a set of allow and deny rules on traffic between subnets, which is the network-layer control described in the teaching text.

questions.prompt: Under a RISE arrangement, where the provider operates the SAP landscape, which design work remains the customer's responsibility according to the layered approach?
choices: Choosing the rented VM hardware generation for the database servers inside the landscape.
Maintaining the physical data centre hardware that hosts the Azure regions.
Running the SAP application patches and kernel upgrades on the operated servers.
Designing the connections into the landscape, identity, and where data is placed.
questions.why: The teaching text states that under RISE the customer's design work centres on the connections into the landscape, identity, and data placement, so that option is the one the customer owns.

questions.prompt: A team chooses a database VM size only because it is the cheapest option with enough memory, and skips SAP's supported-size list. What is the main risk?
choices: The managed disks will be billed twice because the size is not in the price list.
The configuration may fall outside what SAP supports, even if the VM starts and runs.
The network security group rules will stop working automatically until the size is changed.
The VM will run slower only during the first week, then performance returns to normal.
questions.why: The teaching text explains that the VM size is a supported-configuration decision, not only a cost decision, so an unsupported size can place the system outside SAP support even though it appears to work.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would split the Azure compute, network and storage decisions for an SAP RISE landscape, and name one limit or tradeoff of the design you would propose.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would start by splitting the decisions into three layers. Compute: pick VM sizes from the list SAP supports for the database and application servers, because a size outside that list may fall outside supported configurations, and cost alone should not drive the choice. Network: place the landscape in its own virtual network with a subnet per tier, filter traffic with network security groups so the database accepts connections only from the application tier, and connect the corporate network through a private link such as a VPN or ExpressRoute. Storage: put database data and log files on premium managed disks sized for throughput, and use a shared file service where the layout needs one. The tradeoff is that tight subnets and private links add setup work and more rules to troubleshoot, and a larger VM gives headroom but raises cost. Under RISE, I would confirm with SAP which of these parts they manage before we commit.
rubricPoints: Separates the decision into compute, network and storage, each with its own Azure component
Explains that VM sizes should come from SAP's supported list, not cost alone
Describes subnet and network security group rules that limit database access to the application tier
Names a tradeoff, such as added complexity or cost versus headroom, and notes SAP's responsibilities under RISE

suggested.rationale: Tracing which subnets and rules a request passes through builds the layered network reasoning this objective depends on, and the planned path tracer is the closest hands-on match.

lessons.plain: When a company runs a business system for years, the live database keeps growing with old records that people almost never open, yet the company must still keep them for legal or audit reasons. Data archiving means moving those old records out of the live system into cheaper, slower storage, while keeping a clear way to read them when someone really needs them. The live system stays fast and small, costs drop, and the history is not thrown away. Designing it well means deciding what moves, where it goes, and how someone gets it back.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your SAP production database has grown to 20 TB, and most of it is invoices older than seven years that nobody opens. Before reading anything else, what would you propose doing with those old invoices, and what must still be possible for them afterwards?
lessons.teach:
Data archiving means moving records that the business no longer uses day to day out of the live database and into separate storage, while keeping them retrievable. Three terms matter here. The live database is the set of tables the running application reads and writes. An archive store is the separate place old data is written to, often a low-cost cloud storage tier. A retention period is how long a law or company policy says a record must be kept.

It works because the live database is what costs money to keep fast, back up, and restore. Old records that nobody opens still slow backups, copies, and upgrades. Archiving keeps the business history but takes it off the critical path. The application's own archiving process does this in two controlled steps: it writes selected old records into archive files, then deletes them from the live tables only after the files are confirmed complete. Integration means the archived data stays reachable through a read path, so a user can still look up an old invoice.

Worked example. A company wants to archive invoices with a document date older than seven years. Step one: select the matching invoices, say two million rows. Step two: write them to archive files in an archive store, placed in a cool or archive tier. Step three: read a sample back and check that record counts and totals match. Step four: only then delete those rows from the live tables. Step five: confirm that a lookup of an archived invoice still returns the record through the read path.

Common mistake: treating the archive tier as a backup. Archive tiers are cheap to hold but slow to read, because a file may need hours to be brought back online before it can be opened. An archived invoice that a customer-service screen needs in seconds will time out.

Consequence: if the delete step runs before verification, or the read path is never wired up, a month-end report can silently show totals missing years of invoices. Archiving is only complete when the data is removed from the live system, can be read back, and the retrieval time is accepted by the business.

questions.prompt: A regional utility archives smart-meter readings older than three years. It runs the application's archiving process in controlled steps. Step one: select the matching readings, about forty million rows. Step two: write them to archive files in a cool archive store. Step three: [missing step]. Step four: delete those readings from the live tables. Step five: confirm that a customer's historical usage lookup still returns a reading from the archive through the read path. Which choice correctly fills the missing step three?
choices: Copy the archive files into a second archive store in the same archive tier so that a duplicate exists.
Delete the matching rows from the live tables right after the archive files are written, to free space sooner.
Set an archived flag on the rows but keep them in the live tables so the application can still query them quickly.
Read a sample of the archive files back and confirm that record counts and totals match the source before any delete happens.
questions.why: The text says deletion must only happen after the archive files are confirmed complete, and verification by reading back a sample and comparing counts and totals is the check that confirms this before step four.

questions.prompt: In the context of data archiving, what is the live database?
choices: A separate low-cost storage location where old records are written as files for long-term keeping.
The set of tables that the running application reads and writes day to day.
A copy of all records made nightly so that the application can recover after a failure.
The minimum number of years a company policy says a record must be kept before it can be removed.
questions.why: The text defines the live database as the set of tables the running application reads and writes, which is the option that matches that definition.

questions.prompt: A customer portal must show an order's history within a few seconds. The team moves all orders older than two years into an archive tier because the storage is cheap. What is the main problem with this design?
choices: The retention period is too long, so the orders must be deleted before the portal can show them.
The live database will run out of space because archived orders are still counted against it.
Archived files can take hours to be brought online, so the portal lookups will time out and the integration fails its purpose.
Archive tiers cannot store structured records, so the orders will be corrupted when they are moved.
questions.why: The text explains that archive tiers are cheap to hold but slow to read, so a screen that needs data in seconds will time out.

questions.prompt: A company must keep payroll records for ten years under a written company policy, but it rarely opens them after the first year. Which statement correctly describes the retention period's role in this archiving plan?
choices: It is the length of time the records must be kept, and it governs how long the archived data must be retained.
It is the place where the archived payroll files are stored, separate from the live tables.
It sets the speed at which archived files are read back, so a longer period means faster lookups.
It decides which tables count as live, so records are removed from the live database after ten years.
questions.why: The text defines a retention period as how long a law or company policy says a record must be kept, which is what the third choice describes.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate proposes moving all data older than five years out of the SAP database into the cheapest archive storage tier to cut costs. Explain to them, in your own words, what you would check first and what limit or tradeoff they need to accept.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would not start with the cheapest tier. First I would find out which records are actually unused and what the retention rules say about how long each type must be kept, because some records may have a legal period that runs longer than five years. Then I would check the archive process: the old records should be written out and verified as complete before anything is deleted from the live tables. Next, I would confirm the read path, so that someone can still look up an archived record when needed. The main tradeoff is retrieval time. Cold and archive tiers cost less, but a file may need hours to come back before it can be read, so anything the business needs quickly should stay on a faster tier. I would move the data in stages and agree the retrieval time with the business owners before going further.
rubricPoints: Archiving moves rarely used records out of the live database but keeps them retrievable.
Retention rules decide what must be kept and for how long before anything is removed.
Records are written out and verified complete before deletion from the live tables.
Archive tiers are cheap but slow to read, so retrieval time is a tradeoff to agree with the business.
A read path must stay connected so archived records can still be looked up.

suggested.rationale: The core skill is explaining the retention, verification, and retrieval tradeoffs back to a teammate, and no listed mission or engine covers archiving directly.

lessons.plain: SAP RISE is a managed arrangement where a provider runs your SAP systems for you, usually on Azure. Identity and security integration means making sure everyone who signs in to those systems is checked against your company's central user directory, that each person's access is limited to what their job needs, and that the network paths in and out are controlled. Think of a building where the front desk checks badges against the company's staff list and each badge opens only certain floors. You connect the company's existing badge system to the building instead of keeping a separate list of keys inside it. This matters because when someone leaves the company, one change in the central directory should cut off their access to SAP too.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a company already keeps one central directory of staff accounts, why would it be a bad idea to create a separate username and password list inside each SAP system for those same people?
lessons.teach:
An identity provider is the central service that verifies who someone is. On Azure this is often Microsoft Entra ID, the directory that holds your company's user accounts and groups. Single sign-on lets a user sign in once with that provider and then enter SAP without typing a second password. It works through a federation protocol, such as SAML or OpenID Connect, in which the provider issues a signed token that vouches for the user. SAP trusts that token because it was signed by a source it already agreed to trust. Provisioning is the automatic creation and removal of SAP user records based on directory group membership. Authorization is different from authentication. Authentication proves who you are, while authorization is the set of roles inside SAP that decide which transactions you can run. Network controls, such as private connectivity and firewall rules, limit which machines can reach the SAP login ports at all.

Why it works: the directory is the single place where a joiner or leaver is recorded, and SAP accepts signed statements from it. Worked example: Maria joins Finance. Step 1: HR adds her to the directory group FIN-Users. Step 2: provisioning creates her SAP user. Step 3: she opens the SAP logon and is sent to the company sign-in page, where she completes multi-factor sign-in. Step 4: the provider sends SAP a signed token saying she is Maria and belongs to FIN-Users. Step 5: SAP grants the roles mapped to that group.

Common mistake: assuming single sign-on is the whole job, then leaving local SAP accounts with shared passwords active 'for emergencies' or granting broad administrator roles to a large group. Consequence in a running system: when a contractor's directory account is disabled, a leftover local SAP account still lets them in, which is a serious audit finding.

Central identity with mapped roles means a single change in the directory removes access everywhere it is wired, and that outcome holds only when no shadow accounts exist.

questions.prompt: Northwind Freight runs SAP for its depot staff. Dana, a contractor at the Leeds depot, has her directory account disabled on Friday at 17:00, so her company sign-in is blocked. Step 1: her directory account is disabled. Step 2: provisioning removes her SAP user record during the next sync. Step 3: [missing step]. Step 4: when Dana opens the SAP logon on Monday, the sign-in is refused. Which step completes the chain so that no route into SAP remains for her?
choices: Check for and remove any local SAP account for Dana that was created outside provisioning, since a leftover account with a password could still open SAP without the directory.
Leave the firewall rule for the Leeds depot open so the sign-in page keeps loading for her.
Re-add Dana to the directory group so provisioning recreates her SAP user with the same roles.
Widen the roles on her former SAP user so the next audit shows she was fully authorised.
questions.why: A local SAP account that bypasses the directory would let Dana in even after the directory account is disabled, so removing such accounts is what completes the leaver chain.

questions.prompt: A user at a logistics company signs in successfully through single sign-on, but SAP reports that they cannot post a goods receipt transaction. Which statement best explains this?
choices: Authentication failed, so the user never reached the authorization check.
The network firewall blocked the transaction after sign-in finished.
The federation token expired, so SAP ignored the user's group membership.
Authentication succeeded, which proves who the user is, but the roles mapped to them do not include that transaction.
questions.why: Authentication proves identity and succeeded here, while authorization roles decide which transactions are allowed, so a missing role explains the refusal.

questions.prompt: A new branch office in a different city uses a subnet that the central firewall rules have not yet allowed to reach the SAP login ports. Staff there hold valid directory accounts. What is the most likely cause of their failure to reach SAP?
choices: Network controls limit which machines can reach the login ports at all, and the branch subnet is not yet permitted.
Single sign-on has been turned off for their group, so the firewall defaults to deny.
Provisioning did not create their SAP user records, which blocks network traffic.
Their directory accounts lack a federation token, so SAP rejects the sign-in.
questions.why: Network controls such as firewall rules decide which machines can reach the SAP login ports, so an unpermitted subnet fails before identity is even checked.

questions.prompt: A company removes an employee from the directory group SAP-Approvers. During an earlier directory outage, a local SAP account for the same employee was created with a password, and it was never deleted. What is the practical result for that employee?
choices: They can still sign in through the local account, so the central removal does not hold everywhere.
They lose access only to the approval transactions, because the local account has no roles.
They lose all SAP access, because removing the directory group cancels every account they hold.
They are asked to sign in again, after which provisioning deletes the local account automatically.
questions.why: Central identity with mapped roles only removes access everywhere when no shadow accounts exist, and a leftover local account lets the employee sign in regardless of the directory change.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a user who signs in to an SAP system on RISE ends up with their permissions, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying on a central identity provider for that.
lessons.modelAnswer: The user opens the SAP logon and is redirected to the company identity provider, which checks their password and a second factor. The provider then sends SAP a signed token that names the user and the directory groups they belong to. SAP does not check the password itself; it trusts the token, and it maps each group to SAP roles, which decide what transactions the user can run. That separation is the key point: sign-in proves identity, while roles grant permissions. The tradeoff is that the identity provider becomes a dependency. If it is down or misconfigured, nobody signs in, so we need a documented break-glass path with tightly controlled local accounts, and we must review those accounts regularly so they do not become a backdoor.
rubricPoints: Authentication is handled by the central identity provider, and SAP trusts a signed token rather than checking passwords itself.
Group membership in the directory is mapped to SAP authorization roles, which control what users can do.
Provisioning and deprovisioning from directory groups keeps SAP accounts aligned with joiners and leavers.
A limit or tradeoff is named, such as dependence on the identity provider or the risk of leftover local accounts.

suggested.rationale: Explaining the sign-in and permission chain back to a teammate, including its limits, is the core skill here, and no listed mission covers identity for SAP.

lessons.plain: An SAP system runs on a virtual machine in the cloud, which is a rented slice of a computer. Not every size of that rented computer is approved by SAP for running its software. Choosing one means matching the workload's needs for memory, processor cores, and disk speed to a machine size that SAP has tested and certified for that kind of system, such as a database server or an application server. A machine that is too small makes the system slow, and one that is not certified can leave you without SAP support. The skill is reading the requirement first, then checking the approved list before you settle on a size.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your SAP database needs about 1 TB of memory. Before reading any further, what would you check first when choosing a virtual machine size for it, and why?
lessons.teach:
An SAP-certified virtual machine (VM) is a VM size that SAP has validated for running its software, usually for a specific database or application role and operating system. SAP publishes lists of certified sizes, and the cloud provider documents which of its sizes appear on them. A VM size is a named bundle of virtual processor cores, memory, network bandwidth, and disk throughput limits. A memory-optimized size has a lot of memory relative to its cores, which suits in-memory databases. SAP HANA is an in-memory database: it keeps its working data in RAM, so the memory of the VM must hold the database with room for growth and the operating system. Application servers, such as those for SAP NetWeaver, usually depend more on processor capacity and are sized differently.

The method is to start from the requirement, not the price list. Worked example: a HANA database of 1 TB. Step 1: note the memory need from the sizing report, then add headroom for growth. Step 2: filter the VM sizes whose memory is larger than that figure. Step 3: check the SAP certified list for HANA, confirming the size and the operating system are both listed. Step 4: among the sizes that pass, pick the smallest one with sensible headroom. The result is a certified size that fits the data, not just one that looks large enough.

Common mistake: choosing by core count or cost alone, or assuming that a size which ran a test system is certified for production. Consequence in a running system: if the database does not fit in memory, it swaps or fails under load, and a size outside the certified list may be unsupported by SAP, which makes that outage harder to resolve. Choose from the certified list first, then size within it.

questions.prompt: A regional retailer is moving its SAP HANA database to Azure. The sizing report says the database needs 450 GB of memory. The team adds 20 percent headroom for growth, which brings the target to 540 GB. Next they filter VM sizes whose memory is larger than 540 GB. That leaves three sizes with 640 GB, 768 GB, and 1,024 GB. Step 3 is missing from their notes. Step 4 is to pick the smallest size that passes, with the operating system confirmed on the certified list. What belongs in step 3?
choices: Confirm on SAP's certified list for HANA that the candidate size and the chosen operating system are both listed.
Deploy on whichever size ran the retailer's earlier test system, since that size has already worked.
Remove any size whose hourly price is above the cheapest option, then choose from what remains.
Pick the largest of the three sizes, since growth beyond the sizing report is uncertain.
questions.why: Step 3 in the method is to check the SAP certified list for HANA, confirming both the size and the operating system, before the final pick among the sizes that pass.

questions.prompt: What does it mean for an Azure VM size to be SAP-certified?
choices: The size was tested by the cloud provider only, so it can be used for any SAP software.
The size has been validated by SAP for a specific role and operating system, and it appears on SAP's published list.
The size has the highest core count in its family and is priced for enterprise use.
The size has a memory-to-core ratio that SAP recommends, regardless of the database involved.
